title: The Gospel According to Me: Why Self-Authority Cannot Save
excerpt: Modern culture demands we define our own identity and reality. But Scripture reveals why the sovereign self is the oldest idol—and why only Christ can save.
content:
The gospel according to me begins with a simple declaration: I possess the authority to determine who I am. This conviction has become the dominant moral framework of our age. What began as a demand to be left alone has transformed into something far more ambitious—a demand that others affirm whatever identity we declare for ourselves. The individual who once sought freedom from the moral judgments of others now insists that others must validate his own moral judgments about himself. This cultural shift reveals something profound about human nature and exposes why the biblical gospel remains the only message capable of addressing our deepest need.

The New Sacred: Identity as Declaration

Consider the contemporary controversy over transgender identity. Public debate often frames this as a question of courtesy—why not simply use someone's preferred pronouns? But the disagreement runs far deeper than etiquette. It concerns the fundamental authority to determine what a human being is. When a person born male declares himself to be a woman, that declaration makes a claim about reality itself. It asserts that inward psychological experience possesses the authority to supersede the bodily distinction between male and female. And when others are required to affirm that declaration, the claim becomes public and authoritative. The individual's understanding of himself is no longer merely something he believes—it becomes something others must confess.

This demand is especially revealing because it concerns language. A person speaks a declaration about himself, and the world is expected to conform its speech to that declaration. The words of others become instruments through which the declared identity is either recognized or denied. The controversy is therefore considerably more important than a disagreement over grammar. It concerns who has the authority to name reality.

This is why the familiar declaration that "transgender women are women" raises a question that cannot be answered merely by repeating the declaration. What is a woman? If the answer is "an adult human who identifies as a woman," the definition has returned us to the word it was supposed to explain. The category is being defined by an act of identification whose object remains undefined. A definition cannot become adequate merely because questioning it is considered offensive.

The irony is almost unbearable. A culture that insists upon the importance of affirming women finds itself struggling to explain what a woman is. The word remains indispensable even as its meaning becomes disputed. And the dispute exposes something deeper than confusion. The modern self has come to regard the power to define as an expression of freedom. But if freedom means the authority to define reality, then the person who refuses another's definition becomes an obstacle to freedom itself. The consequence is inevitable: the individual who once demanded freedom from external authority begins demanding authority over everyone else.

The War Against the Norm

The same struggle appears in places that initially seem unrelated. A moral framework organized around oppression and liberation can transform ordinary institutions into objects of suspicion precisely because those institutions establish norms. The question becomes less whether a particular institution is good and more whose interests its authority serves.

Within this framework, the family is no longer examined principally as a created relationship involving marriage, procreation, parental responsibility, and the nurture of children. It may be examined as a structure that privileges particular arrangements and imposes expectations upon those who do not conform. The distinction between male and female is no longer received simply as a feature of human embodiment. It may be interpreted as a system of classification that distributes social power. Traditional sexual morality is no longer evaluated principally according to whether its claims about human nature are true. It is examined as a mechanism through which certain identities are privileged and others marginalized. The moral burden shifts. The norm itself becomes suspect.

This reveals a fascinating alliance between two intellectual movements that do not naturally belong together. Marxist approaches to society emphasize the formative power of social structures and material conditions. Expressive individualism emphasizes the authority of inward psychological identity. One looks outward to the systems that shape human beings; the other looks inward to the desires that supposedly reveal who human beings truly are. Yet they cooperate remarkably well when inherited norms are interpreted as instruments of oppression.

The individual discovers an identity within himself. The critical framework identifies the social structures that allegedly prevent its expression. Liberation then requires the reconstruction of those structures. The individual supplies the revelation. The institution supplies the enforcement. And society is expected to conform.

But this framework contains an enormous assumption: it assumes that the norms being challenged are primarily products of human power rather than expressions of an order that exists independently of human preference. What if some norms are not inventions of the powerful? What if the distinction between male and female belongs to the nature of the human body? What if the union of man and woman in marriage is not merely an arbitrary social arrangement (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6)? What if the moral obligations that govern human relationships arise from the character of the Creator rather than the interests of a dominant class?

Then the attempt to liberate humanity from every inherited norm becomes something far more dangerous. It becomes an attempt to liberate the creature from creation itself. And this is where the modern revolution begins to resemble the oldest rebellion in the world.

The Power to Declare

The debates over abortion and sexual identity, though involving different facts and different legal questions, expose a shared problem concerning the authority of human judgment over realities that precede it. The modern self increasingly wants the power to declare—to determine what counts as a person, what counts as a woman, what counts as marriage, what counts as justice, and what counts as harm. And once those declarations acquire moral authority, others may be required to recognize them.

This is not simply the expansion of personal freedom. It is a struggle over the power to name reality. The Christian should recognize the significance immediately.

Naming is not a trivial activity in Scripture. God's creative Word establishes the world. Adam's naming of the animals occurs within the order God has made (Genesis 2:19-20). Throughout Scripture, names identify persons, reveal character, signify covenant relationships, and announce divine purposes. But the authority to name never gives the creature the power to create reality independently of God. Adam names the animals. He does not create them by naming them.

The distinction is fundamental. Human declarations operate within a reality they did not create. A judge may pronounce a verdict that alters a person's legal standing, but the declaration cannot alter the historical events upon which the verdict ought to rest. A mistaken verdict does not become factually true because it carries legal consequences. Marriage vows establish obligations through promises, yet the promises are intelligible because marriage is understood as a relationship possessing a nature and moral significance beyond the private preferences of the people entering it.

Likewise, an individual's declaration may accurately communicate something about his inward experience. But the fact that a declaration communicates a sincere experience does not establish that every proposition contained within it corresponds to reality. Sincerity establishes something about the person making the claim. It does not, by itself, establish the truth of the claim.

The difference between naming and creating is the difference between the creature and the Creator. And our culture is increasingly confused about it.

The Self Without a Fixed Point

The historical development of the sovereign self requires more explanation than a movement from one philosopher to another. The modern self did not simply appear when someone announced that God was dead. It emerged through a long transformation in the way Western people understood authority, identity, and the relationship between inward experience and the world outside them.

Earlier understandings of identity located the individual within a network of relationships and obligations that preceded personal choice. One was born into a family, a community, a history, and a moral order. These relationships could be misunderstood, abused, or unjustly administered, but they were not ordinarily treated as creations of the individual will. The modern psychological self increasingly reverses the direction of authority. The individual looks inward to discover who he truly is and then evaluates the world outside himself according to whether it permits that identity to be expressed.

What once supplied the context within which the self was understood becomes something the self must overcome. The body may be experienced as an obstacle to authentic identity. The family may be experienced as an imposition upon self-determination. Religious authority may be experienced as a denial of personal freedom. Inherited moral obligations may be experienced as oppressive precisely because they were not chosen. The self becomes the standard by which these realities are judged.

But there is an obvious problem. If my inward experience possesses authority over my life, why should it possess authority over yours? If I determine what is true for me, why must you affirm it? If authenticity is the highest good, why is your authentic disagreement with my conclusions morally illegitimate?

The modern self wants to be sovereign over itself while exercising moral authority over others. It wants freedom from judgment and the power to judge. It wants a world without a God who commands, while demanding that its own declarations be obeyed. And the contradiction cannot be resolved by appealing to compassion, because compassion itself requires an account of what is good.

The Exchange

Paul's account of human rebellion in Romans 1 brings the theological structure into focus. "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (Romans 1:18). Notice the order. Paul does not begin with innocent people desperately searching for truth in a universe that refuses to disclose it. He begins with people suppressing truth.

"For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him" (Romans 1:21). Human beings encounter a world that owes its existence to God, yet refuse to respond to him as God. They receive the benefits of creation while withholding the worship due to its Creator. The result is intellectual and moral corruption. Their thinking becomes futile. Their hearts are darkened. Claiming to be wise, they become fools.

Then Paul describes the movement at the center of the passage. They exchange the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal creatures (Romans 1:23). They exchange the truth about God for a lie, worshiping and serving the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25). Human beings do not simply abandon worship. They redirect it. The creature who refuses to worship God does not thereby become free from the need to assign ultimate value. Something else occupies the place of God. Some created thing is invested with an authority it was never meant to possess.

Modern people are inclined to regard themselves as more sophisticated. We do not ordinarily carve an image from wood and ask it to tell us how to live. But we have found a remarkably convenient replacement. We have enthroned ourselves. Our feelings tell us what is good. Our desires reveal who we are. Our experiences establish what others must affirm. The idol is no longer standing on a pedestal in the temple. It is looking back at us from the mirror.

This is why the modern self is not a departure from paganism. It is one of paganism's most concentrated expressions. The creature has become the object of its own ultimate allegiance. And when inward experience becomes the final authority for moral judgment, we have not escaped religion. We have simply changed gods.

The Gospel of Jesus Christ

The Christian account begins with a radically different premise. Human dignity is grounded in the Creator, not in the possession of capacities that make a human being useful, independent, rational, or capable of expressing preferences. The image of God is not awarded to those who have developed sufficiently to exercise particular abilities. It belongs to humanity by virtue of God's creative act (Genesis 1:26-27). A sleeping man does not lose his dignity because he is unconscious. An infant does not lack moral worth because she cannot reason as an adult. Human dependence is not a defect that places someone outside the protection owed to human life.

The gospel does not require the sinner to invent a reality in which he is acceptable. It announces that God has established the only righteousness by which the sinner can be accepted. Justification is not the experience of finally feeling acceptable to God. It is God's forensic declaration that the sinner who believes in Christ is righteous in him (Romans 3:21-26). The declaration does not arise from the believer's inward assessment of himself. It rests upon the righteousness of Jesus Christ, whose obedience and atoning death provide the objective ground of the verdict.

God does not pretend that sin never happened. He does not simply affirm the sinner's preferred understanding of himself. He judges sin and provides the righteousness that the sinner could never produce. The gospel therefore confronts the modern self at precisely the point where the modern self claims ultimate authority.

The modern self declares, "I am what I say I am." The gospel announces what God has done to make sinners righteous in Christ. One is grounded in the authority of the creature. The other rests upon the authority of the Creator.

The Jesus of Scripture is altogether different from the therapeutic projection our culture prefers. He does not arrive to confirm our authority over our lives. He arrives as Lord. He does not invite us to discover an identity independent of God. He calls us to lose our lives for his sake (Mark 8:34-35). And he does not save us by declaring that our feelings were right all along. He saves us by accomplishing in history what our feelings could never accomplish.

We were never meant to create ourselves. We were made to know the One who created us. And until we understand that, we will continue mistaking rebellion for freedom, self-assertion for identity, and the affirmation of our desires for the good news of salvation. The gospel according to me begins with the declaration that I possess the authority to determine who I am. The gospel of Jesus Christ begins with the declaration that I belong to the God who made me. And only one of those declarations can save.

If these are questions you are working through—what Scripture actually says about identity, authority, and the gospel—our Life Groups meet throughout San Diego every week. We would love to think through it together.

title: Their God Is Their Belly
excerpt: We have developed an extraordinary vocabulary for explaining human behavior without ever having to call it sin. We don't gossip anymore â we vent. We don't harbor bitterness â we're protecting our peace. The language is almost ingenious. And it is hiding us from God.
content:
In January 2023, three children were killed in their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts. Cora was five years old. Dawson was three. Callan was eight months old. Their mother was accused of strangling them while their father was away from the house.

The criminal proceedings raised difficult questions â about psychiatric condition, about legal responsibility, about the nature of culpability when severe mental illness may be present. Those questions belong in a courtroom, where evidence can be examined and responsibility determined according to law.

But outside the courtroom, something else was happening.

As the story spread, public discussion shifted toward the suffering of the mother. Her psychiatric history, the pressures of postpartum life, the inadequacy of mental health care â these became the prominent features of the conversation. Many people were genuinely horrified by the deaths. Yet in some of the public reactions, the suffering of the woman accused of killing her children began to overshadow the children themselves. The ability to identify with her experience â exhaustion, anxiety, the overwhelm of motherhood â seemed to become the basis for evaluating what she was accused of doing.

Somehow, compassion was being asked to excuse murder.

I begin with this terrible story not to adjudicate a criminal case or settle a psychiatric debate, but because it reveals something about our collective moral imagination that we have become increasingly unwilling to examine. We have developed an extraordinary sensitivity to the suffering that precedes human behavior, and somewhere along the way we have begun allowing that suffering to determine how the behavior itself ought to be judged. We search for the experiences that explain an action, and when we find them, we are tempted to regard the explanation as an excuse.

We have become so concerned with understanding why people do what they do that we are increasingly uncomfortable asking whether what they do is right.

Of course, most of us have never confronted anything resembling that tragedy. But the moral instinct on display is hardly confined to extraordinary circumstances. We encounter it almost every day. We simply find it considerably easier to recognize when someone else is doing it.

Psychological Fig Leaves

We have inherited an extraordinary vocabulary for explaining human behavior â one that allows us to describe familiar sins without ever having to call them sins.

We don't gossip anymore. We vent. We don't harbor bitterness. We're protecting our peace. We don't refuse reconciliation. We're seeking closure. We don't insist that everyone accommodate our preferences. We're establishing boundaries.

And perhaps we're introverted. Perhaps we genuinely find social interaction exhausting. Or perhaps we're simply rude. Perhaps what we have learned to call a personality trait is sometimes an excuse for refusing to love our neighbor.

The language is almost ingenious. Gossip sounds sinful. Venting sounds therapeutic. We have learned to retain the behavior while changing its moral significance. And because the new vocabulary sounds psychologically sophisticated, we can congratulate ourselves for our self-awareness while remaining remarkably uninterested in repentance.

None of this means that psychological suffering is imaginary or that the categories of mental health are inherently illegitimate. Human beings are complicated creatures, and understanding the circumstances surrounding someone's behavior can be essential to loving him wisely. But understanding why we sin is not the same thing as being absolved of sin. The crisis begins when the explanation becomes a substitute for moral judgment â particularly when the person offering the explanation is ourselves.

When Adam and Eve sinned, they immediately recognized their nakedness and sewed fig leaves together to cover themselves (Gen. 3:7). When God came into the garden, they hid among the trees. The fig leaves could conceal their nakedness from one another, but they could do nothing about their guilt before God.

How much have we really changed? We have traded the leaves of the garden for the language of psychology. We have learned to explain our anger without confessing it, to recount the injuries we have suffered until the injuries we have inflicted disappear from view. Our explanations have become so convincing that we are increasingly capable of hiding our sins from ourselves.

Notice what happens when someone refuses to accept the explanation. Suddenly the person calling for repentance becomes the problem. He lacks compassion. He doesn't understand trauma. He is being judgmental. The person who has done wrong becomes the injured party, and the person who names the wrong becomes the offender. We have become so adept at explaining our sins that we can make the demand for repentance look like the greater sin.

Is it any wonder that so many churches have become reluctant to call their congregations to repent?

When Jesus Sounds Unloving

Pastors have learned what happens when they do.

Tell a congregation that God loves them, that their suffering matters, and that Jesus wants to heal their brokenness, and you will rarely find yourself in trouble. Tell them that they are sinners, that some of their suffering is the consequence of their own disobedience, and that following Christ will require them to deny desires they have spent years learning to regard as essential to their identity â and suddenly you have a pastoral problem. People feel attacked. They wonder whether the church is a healthy environment. And somewhere down the road there is another congregation willing to reassure them that God understands.

But something deeper has happened here. The language of Scripture has become foreign to people who claim to believe it. Not simply because the Bible speaks about sin and righteousness, but because it approaches human beings from the outside in. Scripture does not begin by asking how we feel about ourselves or what we believe we need in order to flourish. It begins with God. He is the Creator. We are His creatures. He determines what is good, what is true, and what it means to be human. Our feelings are real, but they do not possess the authority to define reality.

This is profoundly different from the way we have learned to think. We approach almost everything through the lens of the self â does it meet our needs, affirm our identity, feel authentic? Increasingly we bring those same expectations to Scripture. We want the Bible to speak to us in the language of our psychological experience, and when it refuses, we begin to suspect that its language needs updating.

Sin becomes brokenness. Repentance becomes healing. Sanctification becomes emotional wellness.

These translations may sound compassionate, but they subtly change the subject. The Bible is concerned with our relationship to the God who made us. Our therapeutic vocabulary has a remarkable tendency to return the conversation to ourselves. We can speak endlessly about our need for healing without ever considering that we might need to repent.

The clearest indication of how foreign Scripture has become is how uncomfortable we can be with the words of Jesus himself. He declared that it would have been better for Judas if he had never been born (Matt. 26:24). Judas then experienced overwhelming remorse, confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood, and took his own life. Matthew tells us all of this without suggesting that Judas's anguish somehow altered the moral significance of his betrayal.

Now imagine those words from a contemporary pulpit.

We have become so accustomed to measuring compassion by emotional affirmation that the compassion of Christ himself can appear offensive to us. But compassion cannot be reduced to affirmation. If someone is walking toward destruction, love cannot consist merely of understanding why he wants to go there. The truth may be painful, but withholding it is not mercy â it is simply the preference of a preacher more concerned with how people feel about his words than with whether those words might actually help them.

Paul warned Timothy that a time would come when people would no longer endure sound teaching, but would accumulate teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim. 4:3). Notice the direction of the problem. The congregation develops an appetite, and the teachers learn to satisfy it. Paul called it itching ears. The church has learned to scratch them with psychological fig leaves.

But the Word of God is supposed to be sharp. Hebrews describes it as living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Heb. 4:12). A church unwilling to allow Scripture to wound its assumptions will eventually find itself unable to explain why the gospel is good news â because good news requires a problem serious enough to need it.

Sola Feels

Beneath the therapeutic vocabulary lies an understanding of humanity that has become so natural to us that we scarcely recognize it as an understanding at all.

We assume that the most important truths about ourselves are discovered within our own psychological experience. We believe our desires disclose who we really are, and that personal fulfillment requires us to live in accordance with what we find there. Consider how often we say "I feel" when what we actually mean is "I think." These are frequently judgments about reality presented as descriptions of emotion. And that distinction matters â because feelings have acquired a peculiar immunity from examination. You can challenge someone's reasoning, but when the same judgment is presented as a feeling, disagreement becomes considerably more difficult. How can you tell someone he doesn't feel what he says he feels?

Once feelings are treated as authoritative, they begin making demands on other people. Someone who feels offended expects others to modify their speech. Someone who feels invalidated expects others to affirm his understanding of himself. The discussion is no longer about whether something is true. It is about whether anyone has the right to question what another person experiences as true.

The Protestant Reformation recovered the five solas: Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone, Christ alone, to the glory of God alone. Each directs our attention away from ourselves toward something objectively true. God exists. He has spoken. We are sinners. Christ has accomplished our salvation. These are not religious sentiments whose validity depends upon whether we find them meaningful. They are claims about reality. The gospel is good news precisely because something has happened outside of us â something that remains true regardless of how we happen to feel about it.

And now consider what much of the contemporary church has done with that inheritance.

We have taken a faith grounded in the objective existence of God, the authority of His revelation, and the historical accomplishment of Christ â and increasingly subjected it to the authority of our own psychological experience. We still confess the five solas, but contemporary Christianity seems to have acquired a sixth.

Sola Feels. By feelings alone.

Scripture is authoritative, provided its teaching feels loving. Christ is Lord, provided His commands do not threaten our understanding of ourselves. God receives the glory, provided we remain satisfied with what He has said. We have not formally abandoned the authority of Scripture. We have simply placed another authority above it â one so familiar, so deeply embedded in our understanding of ourselves, that we scarcely recognize its presence. Our feelings have become the measure by which we evaluate the Word of God, rather than the Word of God becoming the measure by which we evaluate our feelings.

We have inherited a faith that tells us what is true. We have turned it into a faith that tells us what we want to hear.

Their God Is Their Belly

Paul has a name for what we have been describing.

Worship.

Near the end of Philippians 3, Paul makes a devastating accusation. Speaking of those who walk as enemies of the cross of Christ, he declares, "Their god is their belly" (Phil. 3:19). Their desires. Their feelings. Whatever they want has become the authority they obey. Paul was writing nearly two thousand years ago, but it is difficult to imagine a more contemporary accusation.

We tend to read a passage like this and think of people enslaved to the most obvious pleasures. But that is precisely the problem. We have spent so long assuming that our feelings reveal who we really are and that our desires deserve to be satisfied that we scarcely recognize these assumptions as assumptions at all. And so we can read Paul's warning about people who worship their appetites without ever considering that he might be describing us.

Paul continues: they "glory in their shame." Once our desires become authoritative, we begin reorganizing our moral judgments to accommodate them. We explain what we once condemned and eventually celebrate what we once regarded as shameful. The church, which ought to know better, has often been eager to help.

What makes the accusation so devastating is that Paul is describing worship. We imagine idolatry as something practiced by ancient people bowing before carved images. But the idol Paul describes is considerably more intimate. It lives within us. It speaks with our voice, shares our preferences, and conveniently agrees with nearly everything we want. We can reject the idols of the ancient world while remaining entirely devoted to our own appetites.

Paul writes these things with tears. He knows where such worship leads. The god of our feelings cannot save us, however sincerely we believe in it. Our desires make terrible masters, and we have become remarkably skilled at confusing obedience to them with freedom.

There is something worth sitting with in that phrase: enemies of the cross of Christ. Not enemies of religion, or of moral tradition, or of the church as an institution. Enemies of the cross. The cross is the place where desire met death â where Christ, who had every right to preserve Himself, gave Himself instead. The cross stands as the permanent refutation of the idea that following your feelings leads to life. And our therapeutic culture, with its insistence that flourishing runs through the satisfaction of desire, is at war with that refutation. Not always loudly. Often tenderly. But at war nonetheless.

Taking Every Thought Captive

Paul tells the Corinthians that Christians are to "take every thought captive to obey Christ" (2 Cor. 10:5). He is confronting arguments raised against the knowledge of God, and that makes his command especially relevant to the world we have been describing. Our age has developed an entire understanding of humanity in which the self possesses the authority to determine what is true. Paul insists that even our thinking must be brought into obedience to Christ. The claims we make about ourselves are no exception.

Consider how foreign that sounds to the modern imagination. We have been taught to trust what arises within us, to discover ourselves through our desires, to regard our feelings as expressions of our authentic identity. Paul tells us to take our thoughts prisoner. He assumes that our thinking must be examined and submitted to someone other than ourselves.

If my feelings determine who I am, then I am bound to whatever I happen to feel. My desires become the measure of my identity, and acting contrary to them becomes a kind of betrayal. I may believe myself free because no one is preventing me from doing what I want â but I have never seriously considered whether I am free to want something different.

Scripture offers an entirely different account of the person. In Romans 7, Paul describes the terrible conflict between what he wills and the sin that dwells within him. He can acknowledge the presence of sinful desires without treating those desires as the final truth about who he is. "It is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me" (Rom. 7:17). Paul is not denying responsibility for his sin. He is not pretending the conflict is imaginary. He feels the power of sin within him. Yet he can speak of it as something dwelling within him without granting it the authority to define him.

This distinction is possible because the gospel has changed something fundamental about the believer. Through the death and resurrection of Christ, the sinner is delivered from sin's dominion and given new life. The Christian continues to experience the desires of the flesh alongside the desires of the Spirit â but those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires (Gal. 5:24). And the fruit Paul speaks of â love, joy, peace â are not merely duties imposed on unwilling people. They are the fruit of a life genuinely transformed by the Spirit of God.

The world tells us that freedom requires obedience to our desires. Scripture tells us that freedom requires deliverance from their mastery.

This is the gospel's extraordinary claim. And it is why Jesus' words in Matthew 16 are not the cruelty they first appear to be. "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me" (Matt. 16:24). To modern ears, that sounds almost unbearable. We have spent our lives being told to discover ourselves, express ourselves, and above all be true to ourselves. And here is Jesus telling us to deny ourselves.

But perhaps we have been reading the command wrong. Perhaps we have become so accustomed to treating our desires as the measure of our humanity that we can no longer imagine what it would mean to be free from them. Perhaps denying ourselves is not the loss of the life we were meant to live, but the beginning of it.

"For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matt. 16:25).

The god of our feelings cannot give us back to ourselves. The belly makes a voracious and unsatisfying deity â always requiring more, never quite delivering the life it promises. Our therapeutic culture has given us a remarkably sophisticated vocabulary for feeding it and almost no language at all for escaping it.

The gospel offers something different: a God who is actually there, who has actually spoken, whose Word stands in judgment over our feelings rather than beneath them, and who calls us â not into the endless project of self-discovery â but into the death that leads to resurrection. That is not the loss of the self. It is the only way to find one worth having.

We have written in this series about the love of God, the mercy of God, and the wrath of God â each attribute belonging to the same God who refuses to be domesticated by our therapeutic expectations. His love does not mean approval of everything we feel. His mercy does not mean our sins are too small to matter. His wrath is not an embarrassment to be softened, but the measure of how seriously He takes the things that destroy us â including the god we have made of our own desires.

If these are questions you're working through â what Scripture actually says about sin, repentance, and the life God calls us toward â our Life Groups gather throughout San Diego every week. We would love to think through it together.

title: The Love of God
excerpt: There may be no sentence in the Bible more familiar â or more easily misunderstood â than "God is love." The difficulty is not that we have no idea what love means. We have too many ideas.
content:
There may be no sentence in the Bible more familiar â or more easily misunderstood â than this one: "God is love" (1 John 4:8).

We use the word love for our children, our spouses, our dearest friends, and â if we are honest â a great many other things that have nothing to do with any of those. The word has become one of the most morally authoritative in modern culture, and simultaneously one of the least defined. Relationships are justified because people love one another. Desires are defended because they arise from love. Moral objections can be dismissed as unloving. The word carries enormous weight precisely as agreement about its meaning has disappeared.

Then we come to Scripture carrying all of that with us and read, "God is love."

It is remarkably easy to reverse the sentence.

Love is God.

Whatever we have already decided love must mean becomes the standard by which God is judged. If God is love, He must approve this. If God is love, He could never command that. Judgment becomes difficult to believe, wrath embarrassing, holiness negotiable. We begin with a creaturely idea â usually one shaped heavily by sentiment and appetite â and reconstruct the Creator until He agrees with it.

John gives us the opposite order. God supplies the content of the word. That distinction changes everything.

Why the Order Matters

Scripture itself knows that things called love can be counterfeit. Love can be hypocritical, which is why Paul tells us it must be genuine (Romans 12:9). It can be claimed while hatred remains in the heart (1 John 2:9â11). It can be reduced to words without costly action, severed from obedience, performed without truth. Paul speaks of love proceeding from "a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith" (1 Timothy 1:5) â because what presents itself as love may have a corrupt source. The biblical writers do not assume that attaching the word love to an impulse sanctifies it.

Neither should we.

This matters especially because the God who is love is also the God we meet everywhere else in Scripture â holy, just, wrathful against evil, sovereign over all things, unchanging. Those truths do not qualify His love. They tell us what it means. His holiness is not something His love occasionally has to overcome. His justice does not pull Him in one direction while His love tugs Him in another. He is not composed of competing tendencies kept in uneasy balance. When He loves, the Holy One loves. The Just One loves. The Almighty loves. The God who needs nothing loves.

Only now are we ready to ask what that means.

A Love That Needs No Explanation Outside Itself

Here is what makes divine love genuinely alien to anything we experience: God does not encounter. Nothing surprises Him into affection. Nothing outside God explains God.

Human love almost always arises within conditions we did not create. We meet someone. Something attracts us â beauty, character, shared history, humor, kindness. Even the most natural and beautiful forms of creaturely love are responses to realities outside ourselves. A parent holds a newborn and loves this child. Two people meet and, over years, come to love each other deeply. We love because something lovely appeared.

God does not work this way.

Moses says something in Deuteronomy that should still sound strange. Israel is God's "treasured possession" among all the peoples of the earth (Deuteronomy 7:6). Why? Moses immediately removes the obvious explanation: "It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples" (7:7). Israel cannot look at election and turn it into a mirror reflecting their own excellence. Then Moses gives the reason: "But it is because the LORD loves you" (7:8).

Why did He love them? Because He loved them. The answer seems circular only if we assume that the final cause of divine love must be something outside God. Moses refuses to provide one. He traces the love backward and, when he reaches God, stops. There is nowhere farther to go.

Paul makes the point painfully concrete. "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). He has already described us as weak and ungodly. Two verses later he calls us enemies reconciled through the death of the Son (5:6, 10). Paul searches the human condition and does not discover the quality that explains saving love. He finds everything that makes the love astonishing.

"We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). The order cannot be reversed. God's love is not His response to ours. Ours is the response.

Before the Foundation of the World

On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus prays to the Father and speaks of "the glory that I had with you before the world existed" (John 17:5). Later He prays that His people may behold His glory "because you loved me before the foundation of the world" (17:24).

We should remain there for a while.

Before there was a world â before stars burned, before angels worshiped, before there was dust from which Adam could be formed, before garden or serpent or fall â love was not absent, waiting for creation to provide its object. Love was already there. The Father eternally delighted in the Son. The Son glorified the Father. This is one place where the Christian confession of the Trinity moves from difficult doctrine into something almost unbearably beautiful.

God does not love creatures because He needed someone to love. He did not create worshipers because heaven was silent and He required applause. Creation is not divine need reaching outward for fulfillment â it is fullness giving. And redemption goes further still: the God who needs nothing has chosen to bring creatures who became His enemies into fellowship with Himself, into the very love that existed before they did.

Jesus prays for this at the end of John 17: "that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them" (17:26). The love with which the Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world â and redeemed sinners are brought into its enjoyment. That is the gospel before the gospel: love older than creation, opened to creatures who deserved none of it.

What Holy Love Actually Looks Like

There is a passage so familiar that familiarity has nearly stripped it of force.

"Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:4â6).

There is an old exercise: put your own name into the passage. [Your name] is patient. [Your name] is kind. [Your name] does not envy or boast. [Your name] is not arrogant. [Your name] does not keep an account of wrongs. We don't get far before the passage begins accusing us. Even where the sentence fits yesterday, it may fail today. Human love can be sincere and still contain astonishing amounts of self.

Now place God there.

God is patient. God is kind. He does not envy, because nothing outside Him could make Him deficient. He does not boast from insecurity, because all glory really is His. He does not rejoice at wrongdoing â He is holy. He rejoices with the truth because truth is never alien to Him. His love does not expire from exhaustion, because God does not run out of Himself.

Modern culture often treats love as the suspension of moral judgment toward the beloved â to truly love someone increasingly means affirming their desires and chosen path without question. But a parent who supplies the addiction destroying his child has not become more loving by removing all judgment. A physician who refuses to treat a malignancy because surgery would be painful is not compassionate. A friend who withholds truth to preserve the relationship loves the relationship more than the friend.

Love seeks the actual good of the beloved. God knows what that good is, and we frequently do not. This is why Hebrews says what sentimentality cannot: "The Lord disciplines the one he loves" (Hebrews 12:6). And why Jesus says to Laodicea, "Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent" (Revelation 3:19). The final triumph of divine love is not that God learns to tolerate everything wrong with us forever. It is that one day there will be nothing left in us that love must oppose.

It is worth reading our earlier post on the wrath of God alongside this one â because a God who is indifferent to evil is not more loving than a God whose wrath opposes it. Indifference is not love. Sometimes it is love's enemy.

The Cross: Where Love Became Visible

To understand what divine love actually cost, we need to go back to a mountain.

In Genesis 22, God tells Abraham: "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love" â and offer him as a burnt offering (22:2). Scripture makes us feel what Isaac is to Abraham before anything happens. The son waited for decades. The son through whom impossible promises had become flesh. And now the father is told to give him.

They climb the mountain together. Isaac carries the wood. Abraham carries the fire and the knife. Then Isaac asks the question that will outlive the scene: "Where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" (22:7). Abraham answers with words larger than he understands: "God will provide for himself the lamb" (22:8).

At the last moment, God stops Abraham. A ram is caught in a thicket. Isaac lives because another dies. But Isaac had asked for a lamb. Abraham names the place The LORD will provide â and the name looks forward. Something about the mountain remains unfinished. Where is the Lamb?

Centuries later, John the Baptist sees Jesus walking toward him and says: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29). The Lamb has finally come.

John 3:16 sends us back to Moriah: "God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son." The son. The only son. The beloved son. At Moriah the hand was stopped. At Calvary there is no ram behind Jesus. No voice comes from heaven saying the sacrifice has gone far enough. The Father gives the Son. John writes: "In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 4:10).

Paul draws the implication we most need to hear: "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" (Romans 8:32). If the Father gave the Son â the greatest possible gift, because there is nothing greater to give â then no dark providence, no painful circumstance, no season of suffering can be honestly read as evidence that divine love has disappeared. The cross has already measured the love. No circumstance can un-give what was given there.

He Loved Me

Paul makes this love uncomfortably personal.

"The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me" (Galatians 2:20).

Not just for sinners. Not just for the church. For me.

Christ did not die for sin as an abstraction. Sin has sinners attached to it. He does not love an approximate version of you â the public self, the presentable version. The God who knows when you sit and rise, who discerns your thoughts from afar (Psalm 139:1â4), who knew Peter's denial while Peter was still promising death â that God is the One who loves. There has never been a moment when God discovered something about one of His children that He did not know when Christ went to the cross. Calvary was not undertaken with incomplete information.

An innumerable multitude across history can each say "He loved me" without the love becoming less personal for any of them. The God who names every star (Psalm 147:4) does not strain to number the hairs on your head (Matthew 10:30). Infinite attention cannot be divided by being given.

And this makes Christian assurance extraordinary. If God's saving love began because you succeeded in becoming sufficiently attractive to Him, you would have to spend the rest of your life protecting whatever quality first attracted His attention. If something in you caused His love, some change in you might remove its cause. But Paul places the ground elsewhere â God chose His people "before the foundation of the world" and "in love" predestined them for adoption "according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4â5). Before obedience. Before repentance. Before usefulness. Before the first breath.

The Christian does not stand upon a love he managed to awaken in God. He stands upon God.

Nothing Can Separate You

Paul ends Romans 8 searching for something that could sever a believer from this love: death, life, angels, rulers, the present, the future, height, depth. He casts the net as wide as language allows â "anything else in all creation" â and finds nothing capable of the task.

"Nothing will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39).

The promises that human love reaches for but cannot finally keep â I will never leave you. I know you completely. You are mine. I would die for you â Scripture places in God's mouth without embarrassment. He says exactly these things. He says them truthfully. He keeps them permanently. "I have called you by name; you are mine" (Isaiah 43:1). "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5). The Son of God loved me and gave himself for me.

We have written in this series about the justice of God, the wrath of God, the wisdom of God, and the mercy of God. Every attribute belongs to the same God. The love of God does not erase His wrath â it makes His wrath meaningful. His love does not ignore His justice â it satisfies it at the cross. His love does not override His wisdom â wisdom is how He accomplishes love's purposes through means we would never choose. The holy love of God is not the softest attribute domesticated for public comfort. It is the most demanding, the most costly, and â because of the cross â the most unshakeable ground any creature will ever stand on.

A Love Greater Than Deserving

There is a deep human instinct, not entirely wrong, that wants to be worth loving. We want divine love to become God's final confirmation of our value â God looked deeper than anyone else, saw what was truly there, and vindicated the suspicion that there had always been something in us worth choosing.

Scripture keeps redirecting this instinct.

The gospel does not cure insecurity by teaching us to think more highly of ourselves. It relocates the weight of assurance entirely outside ourselves. Not: God loves you because you are lovable. But: God loves you, and therefore you are loved. The cross does not flatter us. It does something better â it reveals a love that held nothing back even when the explanation for it could not possibly have been our loveliness. "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."

That is where it ends â and where everything begins.

"We love because he first loved us."

That order is the gospel. And it is the only ground stable enough to build a life on â not the shifting surface of our own faithfulness, intensity, or performance, but the love of the God who loved before the world was made, revealed Himself at a cross, and will hold His own to the very end (John 13:1).

If you're working through these questions with others â wrestling with what Scripture actually says about who God is and what He has done â our Life Groups meet throughout San Diego every week. We'd love to have you join us.

title: The Mercy of God
excerpt: We use the word constantly. We may not know what it means. Mercy begins where our arguments run out â and that is the last place our pride wants to go.
content:
There are words that become smaller through familiarity. Mercy is one of them.

We hear it in prayers, sing it in hymns, place it beside grace, and use it so casually that it can begin to mean little more than kindness. God is merciful â we know this. It belongs among the reassuring things Christians say about Him. If justice makes us uncomfortable, mercy softens it. If wrath seems severe, mercy reassures us that God is not quite as severe as we feared.

Then Scripture shows us mercy.

A blind man hears that Jesus is passing by and cries out: "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" (Luke 18:38). People tell him to be quiet. He cries louder. A tax collector stands at a distance, refuses to lift his eyes toward heaven, beats his breast: "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13). Ten lepers call from a distance. A Canaanite woman follows Jesus crying out.

These people do not sound as though they are requesting something to which they are entitled. Mercy is asked for from below. That is what makes it mercy.

What Mercy Actually Is

Mercy belongs to a family of divine perfections that blur together if we don't distinguish them.

God is good â His goodness is the perfection by which He is infinitely worthy and beneficent, and from which every creaturely good comes. God is patient â He withholds deserved judgment across time, giving space for repentance. God is gracious â grace gives what the recipient does not deserve. It takes the empty-handed and gives them an inheritance.

Mercy has its own character.

Grace gives what we do not deserve. Mercy does not give us what we do deserve. That distinction is simple, but it needs development. Mercy is God's compassionate response to misery, weakness, and need â and in the case of fallen humanity, the misery inseparably bound to guilt. It sees the wretched and bends toward them. It relieves misery, helps the helpless, pardons the guilty, and rescues those with no sufficient resource in themselves.

Psalm 145 says "His mercy is over all that he has made." He feeds creatures that cannot pray. He sustains life that cannot comprehend its dependence on Him. Rain falls on fields belonging to people who curse the God who sends it. Every breath is received. Every meal depends on a chain of providences no eater controls.

The world survives on a generosity it did not create.

But human beings introduce something darker into the picture. We are not merely weak creatures â we are guilty ones. The bird fed by God has not rebelled against Him. The sinner has. That makes every ordinary mercy stranger. The lungs filling with air belong to a rebel. And God fills them anyway.

We Want Innocence, Not Mercy

We have difficulty with mercy because modern people do not particularly want it.

We want innocence. We want to be told that the charges were exaggerated, the circumstances mitigating, our motives understandable, the standards unreasonable, our failures largely products of wounds inflicted by someone else. We may want help. We may want healing. We certainly want affirmation. But mercy is more humiliating â because mercy begins after the question of guilt has already been answered.

Mercy does not say you were innocent. Mercy is what you need because you were not.

We prefer explanations. We explain anger by the provocation that preceded it, lust by loneliness, bitterness by the wound that produced it, pride by the people who failed to appreciate us. Sometimes those circumstances are real. Scripture has room for victims, wounds, oppression, and degrees of culpability. But explanation is not exoneration. A wound can explain why a particular sin became tempting without making the sin righteous. Someone else's guilt does not erase mine.

We resist this because innocence preserves something mercy requires us to surrender: a claim. If I am innocent, I can stand before God and demand vindication. Justice itself requires Him to give it. There is dignity in that posture â I still possess something with which to bargain. Mercy empties the hand.

The tax collector in Jesus' parable does not simply possess fewer credentials than the Pharisee. He has stopped offering credentials at all. He stands at a distance. He will not lift his eyes. "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13). Before a man can hold out an empty hand, he must first admit there is nothing in it. No claim. No hidden righteousness. No argument that God should take into account because he is not as bad as someone else.

The Pharisee has things in his hands. That is his problem. The tax collector finally knows that none of it can save him. And Jesus delivers His verdict: "This man went down to his house justified, rather than the other" (Luke 18:14).

Presuming Upon Mercy

There is a corruption of mercy that may be the most dangerous of all.

"I don't think God would judge me. He's merciful." The sentence sounds humble. It can contain breathtaking arrogance. A divine perfection that should bring the sinner to repentance has become the reason repentance is considered unnecessary. God is merciful, therefore I may continue. God forgives, therefore sin is safe. The sinner has not trusted mercy â he has conscripted it.

Romans 2 refuses the move. Paul asks: "Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?" (Romans 2:4). He continues: "Because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed" (Romans 2:5).

Every additional day of patience can be used in one of two ways. The sinner may see continued life as undeserved kindness and turn toward God â or he may take the absence of immediate judgment as permission to continue. In the second case, mercy is not producing gratitude. It is being converted into presumption.

Scripture never permits us to separate God's mercy from the rest of who He is. When God reveals His name to Moses, He declares Himself "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love" (Exodus 34:6) â and then: "who will by no means clear the guilty" (34:7). God feels no embarrassment placing those truths in the same sentence. Presumption tears it in half. It takes "merciful and gracious" and quietly removes "who will by no means clear the guilty." Then it constructs a god whose mercy means sin cannot finally matter very much. That god is easier to live with. He is also imaginary.

Sovereign Mercy

Even after we understand mercy's proper meaning, we can still imagine it incorrectly.

Romans 9 is a passage we instinctively soften because we understand exactly what it says. Paul is wrestling with God's faithfulness in light of Israel's unbelief. He traces the history of divine election â Jacob rather than Esau, chosen before either had done anything good or bad, "not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11). The objection is predictable: Is there injustice on God's part? Paul answers by quoting God's words to Moses:

"I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion" (Romans 9:15). Then the conclusion: "So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy" (9:16).

There is no responsible way to make that sentence say mercy finally depends upon the creature.

We hear "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy" and immediately ask why God does not have mercy on everyone in exactly the same way. But notice the assumption smuggled into that question. We have begun speaking as though mercy is something every sinner possesses a right to receive. The moment we do that, we are no longer talking about mercy. We are talking about debt.

If I merit something, it is owed to me. Paul makes this explicit: "Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due" (Romans 4:4). Mercy belongs to another moral world. The guilty cannot make mercy obligatory without transforming it into something else. The instant God owes mercy, mercy has disappeared.

The words Paul quotes did not first appear in an abstract theological discussion. They were spoken after Israel worshiped a golden calf â covenant treachery at the foot of the mountain where the covenant was being given. The declaration of sovereign mercy occurs in the presence of people who have forfeited any argument from deserving. There are no morally neutral people in the story. There is a golden calf. Mercy appears after guilt.

The Cost of Mercy

At this point a terrible misunderstanding can enter. If mercy is free, perhaps mercy is easy.

Nothing could be farther from the gospel.

We often think cheaply about mercy because we are the recipients of it. We experience the pardon and not the price. The debt disappears from our account, and because it disappears so completely, we can begin to imagine that it did not cost very much to remove. Mercy is free to the sinner. That does not mean mercy is cheap.

Peter does not allow us to speak vaguely about the price. We were ransomed "not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:18â19). Revelation sings to the Lamb because by His blood He ransomed people for God (Revelation 5:9). Mercy did not come cheaply to God because guilt was trivial. It came through the Son.

This is why the common picture of divine mercy as an indulgent wink is so offensive to the cross. We imagine God looking at sin, sighing affectionately, and deciding not to make a great issue of it. Calvary says God made the greatest issue of it imaginable. If mercy were simply God's willingness to stop caring about justice, there would be no need for Golgotha. If guilt could be dismissed without satisfaction, the agony of Christ becomes inexplicable.

But Scripture gives us another reality. The Father is merciful enough to send the Son. The Son is merciful enough to come. And the judgment mercy spares us from is borne by Him. God does not save by corrupting His own court. He does not call guilt innocence merely because He wants the sinner home. Christ enters the account. The guilt is real. The cost is real. The blood is real. Mercy is free because Another paid what mercy refused to pretend was unnecessary.

The Father of Mercies

If we stopped with everything above, mercy might still feel primarily severe. That would be a failure.

Everything said so far has been necessary because false mercy must be stripped away before biblical mercy can be seen. Mercy cannot be earned. It cannot be demanded. It cannot be presumed upon. It does not abolish justice. But none of those statements tells us how much mercy there actually is in God.

Paul calls Him "the Father of mercies" (2 Corinthians 1:3). The phrase deserves to be heard slowly. Mercies come from Him as from their source. We spend so much time worrying whether God might possibly be merciful that Scripture speaks of Him as rich in mercy, great in mercy, abundant in mercy, the Father of mercies. The Bible's concern is not that mercy in God might run thin if too many sinners arrive at once. The problem was never scarcity in Him. The problem was our claim upon it.

Psalm 103 gives us the fullest picture. God forgives iniquity, heals, redeems from the pit, crowns with steadfast love and mercy (103:2â4). "He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities" (103:10). Then David reaches for distance: "As high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us" (103:11â12). The images resist measurement because measurement is the point. David wants the worshiper to feel how useless ordinary categories have become.

Then the Psalm turns from guilt to frailty: "As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust" (103:13â14). God does not discover our limitations with irritation. He designed the frame. He knows the difference between rebellion and weakness better than we do. He knows when we are exhausted, frightened, confused, grieving, or simply incapable of carrying what we imagined we should be able to carry.

He remembers that we are dust. Sometimes we forget. God does not.

The Father of mercies is not merely willing to cancel punishment at a distance. He has compassion on His children. And in Christ, that compassion comes unimaginably near. The eternal Son entered the condition upon which divine mercy looks. He knows hunger from inside a human body. He knows exhaustion, tears, temptation, betrayal, abandonment, false accusation, and physical suffering. The Father of mercies sent a merciful High Priest who can be touched with the feeling of our weaknesses because He has walked among them.

Therefore Hebrews does not tell frightened sinners to remain at a distance. "Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy" (Hebrews 4:16). A throne is the place of rule and judgment. And we are told to approach it to receive mercy. The confidence cannot be confidence in ourselves â that would contradict everything mercy means. It is confidence in our High Priest.

Before you can cry for mercy, you have to know you need it. And knowing you need mercy means more than admitting that you are imperfect. Almost everyone will concede imperfection because imperfection is easy to survive. The gospel presses farther. You do not need a little help to complete an otherwise successful moral account. You need mercy because if God dealt with you according to your sins, you could not stand.

That is what empties the hand. That is where mercy begins to become beautiful. And that is where the Father of mercies â rich in mercy, great in mercy, the God who sends His Son and His Son who comes â is waiting.

"Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need."

title: The Wisdom of God
excerpt: Power without wisdom is terrifying. Scripture gives us no such God â but it does dismantle everything we think wisdom should look like.
content:
There are few things more dangerous than a powerful fool.

Power amplifies whatever directs it. Give enormous capability to someone who cannot distinguish worthy ends from destructive ones, and his strength becomes part of the danger. Knowledge does not solve the problem either. A person may know an astonishing number of things and still have no idea what ought to be done with what he knows. Intelligence can make foolishness more efficient.

This raises a question Christians rarely ask because the answer seems obvious: Is God wise?

We speak readily of His omniscience, sovereignty, and power. But imagine, for a moment, omnipotence without wisdom â a God capable of accomplishing whatever He wills while incapable of determining what ought to be willed. Sovereignty would make the problem worse. Nothing could restrain Him. Nothing could correct Him. Infinite power placed at the service of an infinitely foolish purpose.

That God would be terrifying.

Scripture gives us no such God. Daniel blesses "the name of God forever and ever, to whom belong wisdom and might" (Daniel 2:20). Paul closes Romans by praising "the only wise God" (Romans 16:27). And then he erupts: "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!" (Romans 11:33).

The moment Scripture declares God wise, it begins dismantling what we think wisdom should look like.

Wisdom Is Not Knowledge

The distinction matters. Knowledge apprehends what is true. Wisdom orders what is known toward a fitting end. Knowledge recognizes the realities involved; wisdom understands what ought to be done with them.

We know the difference intuitively. A physician may possess enormous medical knowledge and still exercise poor judgment with a particular patient. A ruler may possess intelligence, information, and authority and yet ruin a nation because he chooses either the wrong end or disastrous means of pursuing it. Wisdom involves more than information. It involves judgment, proportion, timing, and purpose.

When Scripture calls God wise, none of those can fail in Him. He knows every possible means and every consequence proceeding from every means. He knows every creature, every intention, every relation among events. Yet divine wisdom is more than infinite awareness of possibilities. God also knows the end toward which all things ought to be ordered â because that end does not come to Him from outside Himself.

Paul says God "works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11). That word counsel matters. God's will is not arbitrary power selecting among possibilities. It is the will of the infinitely wise God. He never acts rashly. He never chooses a lesser end because He failed to recognize a higher one. Nothing He wills is foolish.

And because God is simple â not composed of parts â wisdom is not a separate department supervising the rest of His attributes. The God who knows is wise. The God who wills is wise. The God who exercises power is wise. He does not consult wisdom before acting, as though a standard existed outside Him to which His choices must conform. He is wise in Himself.

God Does Not Think Like We Do

Human thought unfolds in time. You began this paragraph without yet having reached its final sentence. Your mind receives information in sequence. Much of what we call thinking consists precisely in that movement â we consider, compare, infer, discover, and revise because the whole is not immediately present to us.

There cannot be such a sequence in God.

Time belongs to creation. God does not move through successive moments gathering information as history unfolds. His knowledge cannot increase because nothing is unknown to Him. He does not reach the end of a chain of reasoning and discover an implication that had not occurred to Him at the beginning. He never encounters a consequence of His own decree and thinks differently because of what He has learned.

God never has a better idea because He never needs one.

All truth is eternally present to the divine mind. Every relation among every truth is known without discovery. When Scripture speaks of His counsel, it reveals real intelligence, purpose, and order â but we should not picture a celestial planning session in which God finally settles upon the most promising proposal. No angel suggested creation. No creature recommended covenant. The incarnation was not Plan B.

God has never received good advice.

The First Suspicion

The human suspicion that God may not be wise enough for us is almost as old as humanity itself.

Genesis 3 is rightly read as a story about disobedience and pride. But notice the language through which the temptation succeeds. The serpent places God's word under suspicion: "Did God actually say?" (Genesis 3:1). Then he places God's motive under suspicion â God is withholding something necessary for human flourishing. And Eve looks again at the tree and sees that it "was to be desired to make one wise" (Genesis 3:6).

The first human rebellion is therefore also an attempted seizure of wisdom from the God who already possesses it perfectly. The irony is devastating. The creature made by Wisdom looks at the world Wisdom created, hears the command Wisdom gave, accepts the interpretation of a serpent Wisdom made, and concludes that she can become wiser by distrusting Wisdom.

That pattern has never disappeared. Sin still contains the judgment that we see enough to know God's way is not best. The adulterer concludes that fidelity cannot be the wisest road to happiness. The bitter person rehearses an injury until forgiveness begins to look foolish. The unbeliever looks at suffering and decides a wise God could not possibly have ordered a world like this.

God speaks. We evaluate. Something still appears desirable to make one wise.

Folly is often the creature's attempt to correct God.

When Providence Looks Foolish

We like divine wisdom until it disagrees with ours.

When providence corresponds to our plans, God's wisdom seems obvious. The job arrives. The diagnosis reverses. The prayer is answered in exactly the form requested. We look backward and say, "God knew what He was doing."

Sometimes He gives no such ending.

The child dies. The marriage does not survive. The cancer remains. The faithful missionary is murdered. Then "God is wise" stops being a pleasant theological proposition and becomes a claim about what just happened.

Much of our anger at providence begins with a hidden assumption. We decide what God ought to be accomplishing and then evaluate His wisdom by His success in accomplishing our objective. We ask whether this event was wise for preserving comfort, extending life, protecting a career, avoiding grief. God may be ordering the same event toward ends we cannot see. Our inability to identify the wisdom of an event cannot establish the absence of wisdom. We are judging a fragment of an order whose whole exists only before the mind of God.

That is precisely where Job found himself.

Where Were You?

Job suffers horribly without knowing why. His children die. His property disappears. His body becomes a source of torment. His friends arrive with a simple explanation â righteous people prosper, wicked people suffer, therefore Job must be wicked. The explanation has the great advantage of making providence manageable.

It is also wrong.

For chapter after chapter Job asks for an audience. He wants to know why. Finally, "the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind" (Job 38:1).

And He does not explain.

"Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" (38:4). "Have you commanded the morning since your days began?" (38:12). "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades?" (38:31).

The questions continue until the sheer size of Job's ignorance becomes almost comic. Job lives inside a world whose ordinary operations he cannot govern â yet he has been attempting to audit Providence. He cannot explain an ostrich. He wants an account of evil.

God could have explained chapters 1 and 2. He does not. Instead He gives Job something more fundamental than an explanation of his circumstances â a clearer apprehension of the One governing them. Job finally says, "I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know" (Job 42:3).

That is not intellectual surrender to irrationality. Job has not learned that reasons do not exist. He has learned that God's reasons are not required to fit inside Job before they can be wise.

That is creaturely sanity.

The Means We Would Never Choose

God has an unsettling habit in Scripture of accomplishing His purposes through means we would reject.

He promises Abraham a son and waits until Abraham's body is as good as dead. He intends to preserve Jacob's family and sends Joseph ahead through betrayal, slavery, false accusation, and prison. He delivers Israel from Egypt and leads them to a place where Pharaoh is behind and the sea is ahead. He chooses Gideon â and then makes his army smaller. He anoints David king and gives him years of caves.

Then Jesus receives word that Lazarus is dying â and waits.

John's wording is almost offensive: "Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer" (John 11:5â6). We expect although. John gives us so. The delay and the love belong in the same sentence.

When Jesus finally arrives, He stands before a grave He deliberately allowed to become occupied â and weeps. That detail protects the doctrine of wisdom from becoming monstrous. Knowing the end does not make Jesus emotionally indifferent to the pain along the road. The tears are real. So is the delay. They belong to the same Christ.

Martha and Mary wanted healing. Jesus intended to reveal resurrection. The means looked foolish because they did not know the end.

Usually neither do we.

The Face of Wisdom

Stephen Charnock made a distinction worth keeping. Creation, he said, shows us the footsteps of divine wisdom. Walk through the world and you find the tracks everywhere â oceans with limits, creatures with habitats, mathematical elegance describing physical realities, living things inhabiting interlocking systems of dependency and provision. "O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all" (Psalm 104:24).

But redemption, Charnock said, shows us the face.

Paul knew exactly how that face appeared to the world. "The word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing" (1 Corinthians 1:18). Jews demand signs. Greeks seek wisdom. Christians preach Christ crucified â a stumbling block to one and folly to the other. The Messiah comes from an unimpressive town. He gathers fishermen and tax collectors. He refuses the political throne when crowds would give it to Him. He allows Himself to be arrested. He dies beneath a sign mocking His kingship.

Stand outside Jerusalem on that Friday without Easter Sunday and ask what part of the scene looks wise.

And this was the plan.

Paul does not rescue Christianity from the embarrassment â he presses directly into it, then identifies the crucified Christ as "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). The world is staring at the Wisdom of God and cannot recognize Him.

What appears to be the destruction of God's purpose is accomplishing it. Death becomes the means by which death is defeated. Divine justice is satisfied while mercy is extended. The apparent victory of Satan becomes the instrument of his defeat. Shame becomes the road to glory. The grave itself becomes the place from which resurrection is revealed.

No creature would have devised this. No creature could have accomplished it if he had.

The cross does not merely show that God can recover from evil. It shows that evil never forced Wisdom to improvise. The Lamb was foreknown "before the foundation of the world" (1 Peter 1:20). The cross belongs to the counsel. Redemption is not evidence that God is exceptionally good at recovering from disaster.

Living in Friday

The Christian lives in an awkward place. We live after the resurrection, so we have seen enough of God's purpose to know something about His wisdom. But we live before the consummation, which means we still inhabit stories whose endings remain hidden.

Joseph understood this long before us. At seventeen he receives dreams suggesting exaltation. Then his brothers throw him into a pit. He is sold into Egypt, falsely accused, imprisoned, forgotten. None of those moments, considered in isolation, carries an obvious explanation of what God is doing.

Then Pharaoh dreams. Joseph rises. The family is preserved. Only after decades can Joseph say, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). He does not say his brothers' evil became good. Their intention remains evil. God's intention in governing the same event was already good while Joseph sat in the pit.

The pit belonged to the wisdom before Joseph could see Egypt.

That is precisely where faith becomes difficult. We want God to vindicate His wisdom while we are still in the pit. Sometimes He allows us to see Egypt. Sometimes He does not. Some Christians die with questions that will never be answered inside this age.

This is why the cross matters so much to the doctrine of wisdom. It gives us a completed pattern by which to interpret incomplete ones. Friday looked like failure because Sunday had not yet arrived.

We live in a great deal of Friday.

Christ Our Wisdom

God's response to the problem of wisdom is not, finally, a better explanation. It is a Person.

Paul tells the Corinthians that God has made Christ "our wisdom and our righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1 Corinthians 1:30).
