John opens his Gospel before Bethlehem, before Mary, before Rome or Israel or creation itself: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1).

The Logos â eternal Reason, divine Wisdom â is not a rational principle within the universe. He made the universe. And then: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14).

Wisdom came down.

The first human act of rebellion was a reach for wisdom independent of God. The gospel reveals the opposite movement. Wisdom is received when the creature returns to God through the One who is Himself the Wisdom of God. "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom" (Proverbs 9:10) â not because fear and wisdom are somehow separate, but because wisdom begins when the creature recognizes that the God who speaks sees what the creature cannot.

Eve reached because she thought she could see enough. The wise person fears God because he knows he cannot.

The One who never needed counsel came among fools. The One whose understanding cannot increase genuinely grew in human wisdom. The One who orders every end and every means allowed Himself to be led outside Jerusalem as though events had escaped His control.

They had not.

The cross was not the collapse of Wisdom. It was the masterpiece.

There will still be providences we never understand in this life. Some losses will never resolve into neat testimonies. Some prayers will appear unanswered until death. Sometimes faith says only, I do not know.

But Christianity gives us something better than a fabricated explanation. We know something about the One whose reasons remain hidden. The One whose wisdom we are being asked to trust is holy enough never to corrupt His purpose, just enough never to wrong us, faithful enough never to break His word, good enough that malice is impossible, and wise enough that no deficiency in judgment can enter the order of His works.

We may not know what He is doing.

We know who is doing it.

And Wisdom has a face.

"The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). If human beings had invented divine wisdom, we would never have written this story â the eternal Logos appearing first as an infant, spending decades in obscurity, working with His hands, touching lepers, weeping at a tomb He could have prevented from becoming occupied, then led outside Jerusalem as a condemned criminal while the people who believed themselves wise watched Him die.

That is the face of Wisdom. And it should permanently unsettle our confidence in our ability to recognize wisdom by appearance.

The fruit was taken. The Son was given. The world called it foolishness.

God called it the plan.

title: The Wrath of God: What the Bible Actually Says (And Why It Matters)
excerpt: We are comfortable saying God is love. We grow uncomfortable when Scripture speaks of His wrath. But God shares none of our embarrassment â and neither should we.
content:
There are attributes of God Christians instinctively defend, and attributes for which we instinctively apologize.

Wrath belongs to the second category.

We are comfortable saying that God is love. We sing about His faithfulness, rest in His goodness, appeal to His mercy, ask for demonstrations of His power. But when Scripture speaks of His anger, fury, vengeance, and wrath, our posture changes. We lower our voices. We begin explaining. We hurry toward qualifications â assuring everyone that God is not really like the angry gods of pagan religion, which is true, and then sometimes continuing to qualify until very little anger remains.

God does not share our embarrassment.

He speaks about His wrath with a directness that can make even Christians uncomfortable. "God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psalm 7:11). Nahum opens with words that sound almost impossible to modern ears: "The LORD is a jealous and avenging God; the LORD is avenging and wrathful" (Nahum 1:2). Paul says plainly, "the wrath of God is revealed from heaven" (Romans 1:18). Revelation ends the biblical story with the nations facing "the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).

Scripture makes no attempt to hide any of this.

That should make us suspicious of our discomfort before it makes us suspicious of God. If God is not ashamed of His wrath, why are we?

What Is the Wrath of God?

We must define this carefully, because the word wrath immediately carries the debris of human experience.

Divine wrath is God's holy, personal, settled opposition to evil and His righteous determination to punish those who persist in rebellion against Him.

Each part of that definition matters.

Wrath is holy because nothing impure produces it. There is no wounded vanity in God, no insecurity, no loss of control, no irrational surge of emotion. God does not become angry because events have overwhelmed Him or because someone has touched a nerve. His wrath arises from the same perfect nature from which His goodness, holiness, and love arise.

Wrath is personal because sin is personal. Evil is not merely a violation of an abstract moral code. Sin is rebellion against God. David understood this even after sins that obviously harmed other human beings: "Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight" (Psalm 51:4). Every sin is committed within God's world, against God's authority, beneath God's gaze, using life and strength borrowed from God Himself.

Wrath is settled opposition because God does not lose His temper. He knows completely, evaluates perfectly, and opposes evil without confusion. Nothing needs to happen inside God before He becomes capable of recognizing evil for what it is.

This is what distinguishes divine wrath from the human anger we know so well. We have seen fathers lose their tempers, crowds become mobs, rulers turn vindictive, and ordinary people say things in ten seconds of rage that cannot be repaired in ten years. Our anger is frequently disproportionate to the offense, distorted by pride, intensified by ignorance. We know what it is to be angry because our ego has been bruised or our desires frustrated.

Then we take that experience, enlarge it infinitely, and call the result divine wrath.

That is the mistake.

He Feels Indignation â Every Day

It is easier to imagine God judging sin than feeling anger toward the sinner. Judgment can be made abstract â a law, a scale, a sentence, a perfectly functioning moral order where consequences follow violations with mathematical precision. There is something reassuringly impersonal about such a universe. The law may condemn me, but the law does not know me. Gravity can kill me, but gravity has nothing against me.

The Bible will not allow us that distance from God.

"God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day" (Psalm 7:11). The sentence joins precisely what we are tempted to separate. His judgment is righteous, and His indignation is real.

What makes His wrath unlike ours is not that ours is passionate while His is cold. God's wrath possesses a purity our passions never achieve. His anger never clouds His judgment because His anger agrees perfectly with His judgment. His hatred never makes Him unjust because He hates only what is worthy of hatred. His vengeance cannot exceed what evil deserves because omniscience knows the offense completely and justice measures it without error.

Nothing in God needs to cool down.

That fact should frighten us more than the image of uncontrolled rage. A furious man may eventually regain perspective. God already has perfect perspective. Time will not soften a mistaken first impression â there was no mistake. Further evidence will not reveal mitigating facts He overlooked â He overlooked nothing.

There is no calmer God behind the anger to whom we might appeal.

His anger is the anger of the holy God.

The Wrath of God Is Good

Imagine a man watching someone brutalize a child. He understands exactly what is happening and possesses the power to intervene â yet nothing rises within him against the evil. He watches calmly and later explains that anger is beneath him.

We would not praise his emotional maturity. We would question his goodness.

There are realities toward which moral neutrality becomes immoral. Now remove from anger everything that makes our anger dangerous â remove ignorance, insecurity, pride, wounded ego, impulsiveness, and the desire to inflict more suffering than an offense deserves. Remove the possibility of directing anger toward the wrong person.

What remains is not indifference. It is righteous opposition to evil.

A god who could look upon rape, murder, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and every secret corruption of His creatures with perfect detachment would not be morally superior to the God of Scripture. He would be morally deficient. Perfect goodness requires perfect opposition to what destroys and defiles the good.

The difficulty appears when we agree with that principle and then quietly reserve the right to identify which evils deserve divine anger. We approve of God's wrath against the sins we already hate. Scripture includes the ones we excuse.

Romans 1 traces the human catastrophe back past the spectacular sins to something we barely recognize as deserving wrath: human beings "did not honor him as God or give thanks to him" (Romans 1:21). They exchanged His glory for images and "the truth about God for a lie, worshiping and serving the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:23, 25).

Idolatry is the architecture of sin. And God's wrath is what perfect holiness feels toward that rebellion.

Against Whom Is God Angry?

A familiar Christian expression â God hates the sin but loves the sinner â is trying to preserve something true. But Scripture refuses to locate all divine opposition in an abstraction called sin while leaving the person who sins untouched.

"The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all evildoers" (Psalm 5:5). "The LORD tests the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence" (Psalm 11:5).

Sin does not go to hell. Sinners do.

Jesus says evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, coveting, deceit, envy, slander, pride, and foolishness come "from within, out of the heart of man" (Mark 7:21â23). The sinner cannot finally introduce his sin to God as though presenting a third party.

That is why wrath falls upon persons.

Already Condemned â What John 3:16 Doesn't Tell You Alone

"For God so loved the world." We know the sentence before John 3:16 is finished. And the verse is rightly precious. But familiarity has allowed us to imagine the world in John 3 as though humanity stood in neutral territory while God offered eternal life as a better destination.

Jesus describes the situation differently.

"Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already" (John 3:18).

Already. The Son enters a world under sentence.

Paul then takes what Jesus says and makes it even more personal. "We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind" (Ephesians 2:3). He could have said we committed acts deserving wrath â that would have been severe enough. Instead he describes what we were. Jew and Gentile, religious and irreligious, respectable and debauched, gathered under one description. Paul himself stands inside it.

So do we.

Only now are we ready to meet Jesus.

The Wrath of the Lamb

Our instinct at this point may be to expect Jesus to soften what has come before. The Old Testament gives us Sinai, flood, fire, and judgment. Then Jesus arrives â touching lepers, receiving children, eating with sinners, forgiving prostitutes. Even Christians who would never explicitly oppose the Son to the Father can begin to feel that Jesus reveals the kinder side of God.

But we have not noticed enough of Him.

There is a form of idolatry that requires no statue. We can construct a Christ from the sayings our culture already approves â and because every piece came from the Gospels, mistake the selection for Jesus Himself. The Jesus who warns about hell, pronounces woes upon cities, speaks of outer darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth, and unquenchable fire becomes increasingly difficult to fit into the portrait.

Then He says something that should stop us: "I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled!" (Luke 12:49).

The difficulty is not merely the fire. It is the desire. Jesus does not speak like a reluctant bureaucrat announcing a penalty He finds personally distasteful.

John sees Him again decades later â in Revelation â with eyes "like a flame of fire," feet like burnished bronze, a voice "like the roar of many waters," and a face "like the sun shining in full strength" (Revelation 1:14â16). John, who had reclined beside Jesus at supper, falls at His feet as though dead.

Then, as the Lamb begins opening the seals, creation itself recoils. Kings, generals, the rich and powerful, slave and free â all cry for the mountains to fall on them rather than face "the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).

The phrase is almost an oxymoron. Lambs are vulnerable. Lambs are sacrificed. Lambs bleed.

This Lamb is angry.

There are not two Jesuses. There is no gentle Christ at Calvary who reluctantly becomes severe when history exhausts His patience. The compassion and the wrath belong to the same holy Person.

The Cup: What Happened at Gethsemane

Gethsemane is frightening long before the soldiers arrive.

Jesus tells His disciples, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38). He falls on His face and prays: "My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me" (Matthew 26:39).

The cup is not an unexplained image. Israel's Scriptures had already filled it. "In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine," Psalm 75 says, "and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs" (Psalm 75:8). Isaiah speaks of "the cup of his wrath" (Isaiah 51:17).

Jesus knows what is in the cup. Wrath.

This is why physical descriptions of crucifixion, however horrific, can never reach the center of Calvary. Rome had crucified others. It would crucify many more. Christians would later face torture and death with remarkable courage. Yet in Gethsemane the sinless Son falls upon His face in anguish before what approaches.

The nails are coming. But so is the cup.

The Son has known the Father's love without beginning. There has never been alienation within the life of God â never suspicion, hostility, distance, or moral disapproval between Father and Son. Now the incarnate Son takes the place of enemies. Our sins are reckoned to Him. He stands as covenant representative beneath the judgment they deserve.

"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).

We can say what Scripture gives us to say. The sins are ours. The Substitute is willing. The judgment is real. The cup is wrath.

And He drinks it down. All of it.

Propitiation: The Word That Changes Everything

Christ's sacrifice satisfies divine wrath. God put Him forward "as a propitiation by his blood" (Romans 3:25), and John says that God "loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 4:10).

That second text is especially important because it refuses to assign love and wrath to different persons of the Trinity. The Father loves â and therefore sends the Son as propitiation. The wrath being satisfied belongs to the holy triune God, and the love providing satisfaction belongs to that same God.

Pagan propitiation moves in the opposite direction: human beings offer something to angry gods to make them favorable. The gospel begins with God's own initiative. The offended God provides the sacrifice by which His enemies are reconciled to Him.

God's love does not appear after His wrath has been persuaded to leave. His love gives the Son who drinks the cup.

And because the Son Himself possesses the holiness from which divine wrath proceeds, He is not an innocent outsider dragged into a quarrel. He is the offended God who has taken our nature, the willing Substitute who stands where His people should stand â and the Lamb whose own wrath will one day terrify the nations.

The personal character of wrath has led to an even more personal salvation. God does not merely provide a way around Himself. He gives Himself.

No Wrath Remains for Those in Christ

For the Christian, this has enormous pastoral consequence.

"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1).

God has not justified His people while retaining a portion of His condemning anger in reserve. The believer's failures can bring discipline, grief, and painful correction â Hebrews is explicit that "the Lord disciplines the one he loves" (Hebrews 12:6). But fatherly discipline and judicial wrath belong to entirely different relationships.

Christ drank the cup.

We should be very careful before adding anything to that sentence. The Christian does not receive the final mouthful on his worst day. The cup does not move back and forth between Christ and His people according to the quality of their sanctification. If condemnation could return, the cross would not have exhausted it.

There is no wrath left for the believer to bear.

The enemy has become a son. That is reconciliation.

The Wrath That Remains for Everyone Else

John 3 closes the circle with uncomfortable precision. The chapter containing "God so loved the world" ends: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36).

Remains.

The gospel does not create danger by placing an otherwise neutral person before a new religious decision. The danger is already there. Condemnation is already there. Wrath remains.

Christ is not one possible enhancement to human existence. He is the only refuge from the holy God against whom we have sinned. And we now know something about that refuge that makes unbelief particularly serious: the refuge is the Lamb. The blood that saves from wrath belongs to the One whose wrath will one day be revealed. There is nowhere else to go.

Learning to Delight in the Wrath of God

God is not embarrassed by His wrath. Can we move beyond embarrassment too?

This does not mean Christians should cultivate pleasure in the suffering of the wicked. Scripture gives no permission for that. Paul speaks of his unbelieving kinsmen with "great sorrow and unceasing anguish" (Romans 9:2). Jesus weeps over Jerusalem while announcing judgment. A Christian who speaks lightly about hell has probably ceased to feel both the horror of judgment and the wonder of having escaped it.

Yet Revelation shows that grief over the lost and delight in God's righteousness are not finally contradictory. When Babylon falls, heaven cries: "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just" (Revelation 19:1â2).

They are not praising suffering as suffering. They are praising God because every lie has finally met truth, every hidden cruelty exposed, every victim vindicated, every idol fallen. Satan does not negotiate a settlement. Evil does not receive an eternal corner in which it may continue existing because judgment would have been too severe.

God's hatred of evil is good. His vengeance is good. His wrath is good.

We struggle to say that now because we are still sinners, our anger is corrupt, and we know what we ourselves deserved. But none of those deficiencies belongs to God. There is no blemish in Him for eternity to explain away. We will never discover that God was slightly too angry about sin.

We will see more clearly. And then we will understand something we can only begin to understand now: the wrath that once frightened us because it was directed toward us will become part of what makes the holiness of God beautiful to us â because we will know where ours went.

The Wounds of the Lamb

Scripture gives us one Christ. He receives children and terrifies demons. He touches lepers and pronounces woes. He weeps over Jerusalem and foretells its destruction. He forgives sins committed against Him. He longs for the fire to be kindled. He kneels before the cup. He drinks it. He dies beneath judgment. He rises. He offers peace to His enemies â and ascends to heaven, where He waits for the appointed day when the Lamb who was slain will judge the world.

The scars remain.

For the unbeliever, those wounds will testify that the God who judges did not remain distant from sinners. The One before whom the nations stand is the One who entered their world, took flesh, warned them, wept, bled, died, rose, and sent a message of reconciliation throughout the nations. The wrath of the Lamb will never mean the Lamb was unwilling to save.

But for the Christian, the wounds say something else. They tell us where the wrath went.

We were children of wrath. We were condemned already. We were enemies of the living God. God knew us completely, and the evil He hated was in us. His holy indignation rested on our relationship with Him.

Then the One we had offended came for us.

And because the offense was personal, the reconciliation is personal too. God has not merely ceased punishing us. The Judge has not simply stamped acquitted across the record and dismissed us from His courtroom. The God whose wrath rested upon us has brought us near.

Enemies sit at His table. Children of wrath become children of God. Those who deserved the cup of wrath will drink the wine of His kingdom.

Then Zephaniah â a book that opens with terrifying language about the wrath of God â closes with something almost impossible to take in:

"The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing." (Zephaniah 3:17)

God sings over His people. Not reluctantly. Not with the measured approval of a judge acknowledging that legal requirements have technically been satisfied. He rejoices. He exults. The language is as personal as the language of wrath was personal.

Reconciliation does not merely mean God no longer feels wrath toward us. He delights in us.

The wrath of God is as pure as His holiness, as right as His justice, as unwavering as His immutability â and as worthy of Him as every perfection we find easier to love.

For those outside Christ, that remains terrifying. It should.

But those in Christ will stand before the same God and discover that reconciliation was every bit as personal as wrath.

The Lamb has wrath. The Lamb has wounds. And over those purchased by those wounds, God sings.

title: The Justice of God
excerpt: We want Godâs justice when weâve been wronged. We grow considerably less enthusiastic when the scales turn toward us. What the Bible teaches about divine justice changes everythingâespecially at the cross.
content:
There are some attributes of God that we instinctively want near us. We want His goodness near us, His faithfulness beneath us, His power working for us. Justice is more complicated. We want it when we have been wrongedâwhen the powerful exploit the weak, when corruption goes unpunished, when evil appears to prosper. Something in us rises at the thought that wickedness might finally win, that accounts might never be settled.

We become considerably less enthusiastic when the scales turn toward us.

That instinct reveals something true. We know enough about justice to appeal to it, but we are not ourselves just enough to welcome its perfect application. When our own lives are placed upon the scales, we introduce circumstances, intentions, mitigating factors, and mercy. The uncomfortable truth beneath all those qualifications: we do not naturally desire justice in the abstract. We desire a judgment favorable to us.

God does not.

What Is the Justice of God?

âThe Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is heâ (Deuteronomy 32:4).

That is a more frightening statement than it first appears. There is no crookedness in God. None. And because there is none in Him, there can be none in His judgments.

Scripture speaks of Godâs righteousness and justice in overlapping ways. The Hebrew tsedeq (righteousness) and mishpat (justice) often appear together: âRighteousness and justice are the foundation of your throneâ (Psalm 89:14). Godâs righteousness concerns the perfect rectitude of His nature. His justice is that righteousness exercised in moral judgment. Because God is righteous, He invariably judges rightlyâapproving what ought to be approved, condemning what ought to be condemned, rendering according to truth, never bending judgment through ignorance, corruption, fear, or favoritism.

Justice is also distinct from wrath, though the two necessarily meet. Wrath is Godâs holy anger and settled opposition toward evil. Justice concerns the rightness according to which evil is judged. In God, unlike in us, His wrath is always just, and His justice is never distorted by passion.

The Ground of Justice

Every moral claim quietly assumes a standard. When we say a board is crooked, we compare it to straightness. When we call a judgment unjust, we appeal to something beyond the judge. Moral judgments work similarlyâwhen we say that a man ought not abuse a child, that a government should not murder the innocent, we mean more than personal preference. We are claiming there is a moral reality to which conduct must conform.

Where does that ought come from?

It cannot come from us. If individuals create morality, the murderer and victim simply have conflicting preferences. Society cannot be the final source eitherâsocieties themselves become unjust. Slavery doesnât become righteous because a civilization legalizes it. And if power defines what is right, we havenât explained justice at all. Weâve merely renamed victory.

Every genuine ought therefore points beyond the creature.

Christianity does not solve this by placing an abstract law above God, as though righteousness existed somewhere outside Him as a standard He must meet. But if justice were simply whatever an arbitrary divine will happened to command, calling God just would tell us almost nothingâcruelty could become justice tomorrow if God decided to call it that.

Scripture gives us neither extreme. Justice is grounded in Godâs own perfect nature. âThe LORD is righteous in all his waysâ (Psalm 145:17). âThe LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deedsâ (Psalm 11:7). God is not measured by the straight line. He is why there is a straight line.

This means God cannot be slightly unjust. We have almost no analogy for it. Human beings can be generally fair while still rendering a bad decision in a moment of weakness or prejudice. We speak of better and worse systems of justice because human justice exists on a spectrum. God does not inhabit the good end of that spectrum. One unjust judgmentâone innocent person knowingly condemned, one fact overlooked, one judgment distorted by partialityâwould require God to cease being the God Scripture reveals. âThe judgments of the LORD are true, and righteous altogetherâ (Psalm 19:9). The scales do not tremble in His hand.

The Judge Who Sees Everything

The traditional image of justice is blindfolded. Lady Justice holds her scales while her covered eyes symbolize impartialityâshe must not know whether the person before her is rich or poor, friend or enemy. Human justice sometimes protects itself by refusing to see what might improperly influence judgment.

Godâs justice is impartial for the opposite reason. He sees everything.

âNo creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give accountâ (Hebrews 4:13). God knows the deed and the intention. He knows what was done publicly and what was concealed. He knows the outward act of generosity and the vanity secretly feeding upon the applause. He knows what warnings we ignored and what motives we have successfully hidden even from ourselves.

This omniscience makes His justice terrifyingly exact. Scripture speaks of degrees of accountability: Jesus says it will be âmore bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrahâ than for towns that witnessed His works and rejected Him (Matthew 10:15). God âwill render to each one according to his worksâ (Romans 2:6). Divine judgment is precise without being crude.

And God shows no partiality. He cannot be bought, intimidated, or pressured by a crowd. He does not adjust His verdict because the defendant is important, and He does not condemn someone merely because condemnation would satisfy public outrage. He has no constituency to appease and no election to survive. There is something wonderfully clean about divine justiceâand something terrifying about its cleannessâbecause every technique by which human beings evade human judgment is useless before Him.

When Justice Seems Absent

The world frequently does not look just. The wicked prosper. The righteous suffer. Abusers die peacefully in old age. Faithful people are buried young.

Psalm 73 is written from inside this scandal. Asaph nearly loses his footing when he sees âthe prosperity of the wickedâ (Psalm 73:3). For a moment he concludes, âAll in vain have I kept my heart cleanâ (Psalm 73:13). That is the pressure injustice places on faithâif righteousness and wickedness receive the same end, righteousness begins to look foolish.

But Scripture does not solve this by pretending the observation is false. Habakkuk asks why God tolerates wrong while âjustice goes forth pervertedâ (Habakkuk 1:4). The martyrs beneath the altar cry, âO Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood?â (Revelation 6:10). They do not ask whether God will judge. They ask how long.

The apparent absence of justice in history becomes an argument for judgment beyond history. Ecclesiastes sees wickedness where justice ought to be and concludes, âGod will judge the righteous and the wickedâ (Ecclesiastes 3:17). Delay is not acquittal. Justice has an appointment.

The Great Problem: How Can a Just God Forgive?

Here is where the doctrine of divine justice moves from abstract to urgent.

We usually approach salvation by asking how a loving God could condemn sinners. Paul approaches the gospel from the opposite direction: How can a just God forgive them?

Imagine a judge before whom overwhelming evidence establishes a murdererâs guilt. Witnesses testify. DNA confirms. Video records it. The defendant confesses. Then the judge smiles and says, âI am merciful. You may go.â

We would demand his removal. Mercy that simply ignores justice is corruption. Scripture itself says so: âHe who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORDâ (Proverbs 17:15).

Read that carefully. God calls the justification of the wicked an abomination. Then Paul announces that God âjustifies the ungodlyâ (Romans 4:5). There is the crisis at the heart of the gospel. How can God do what He Himself declares abominableâand remain righteous?

The Cross: Just and Justifier

Paul does not leave the tension unresolved. God put Christ forward âas a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith.â And here is the key: âThis was to show Godâs righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sinsâ (Romans 3:25).

The cross demonstrates more than Godâs love for sinners. It vindicates His righteousness in having forgiven them.

Romans 3:26 states the purpose with extraordinary precision: the cross occurred âso that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.â God remains just while He justifies. His attributes are not competing departments negotiating a compromise. Mercy does not persuade justice to leave the courtroom. Justice receives everything justice requiresâand the sinner receives mercy.

The explanation is substitution.

âHe was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquitiesâ (Isaiah 53:5). âThe LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us allâ (Isaiah 53:6). God made Him âto be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of Godâ (2 Corinthians 5:21). Christ âsuffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to Godâ (1 Peter 3:18).

The cross is mercy for us because it is judgment upon Him. The guilt remains what it is. The judgment remains what it ought to be. Christ stands where His people should stand. And His final declaration carries the full weight of that reality: âIt is finishedâ (John 19:30). Nothing remains unpaid.

Justification: More Than Forgiveness

The gospel does something equally staggering in the other direction. The guilt of the sinner is reckoned to Christâand the righteousness of Christ is reckoned to the sinner.

This is justification, and justification is a courtroom word. God does not first transform the sinner into a sufficiently righteous person and then pronounce him righteous upon inspection of the improvement. He âjustifies the ungodlyâ (Romans 4:5)âthe verdict comes while the ground of righteousness remains entirely outside the sinner, in Christ.

This is bigger than forgiveness. Forgiveness alone would be enough to occupy eternityâs praisesâevery crime removed, every debt canceled, every accusation answered. But justification goes further. The sinner leaves the courtroom with a righteous standing before God he did not produce and cannot improve upon. God receives him according to the righteousness of His Son.

âFor our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of Godâ (2 Corinthians 5:21). Our guilt reckoned to Him. His righteousness reckoned to us. The verdict is judicial, but it is not imaginary. The scales remain straight in both directions.

This is why the Christian can say: âThere is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesusâ (Romans 8:1). Not eventually. Now. The verdict has already been rendered. Justice has already spoken.

He Pays or You Do

That makes unbelief far more serious than simply declining a religious offer. If Christ is the only righteous satisfaction for guilt, to reject Christ is to choose to stand before perfect justice without Him.

There is no third option. Either Christ bears the judgment or the sinner does.

Jesus gave a warning that sounds almost mundane until you understand the courtroom it points toward: âCome to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judgeâ (Matthew 5:25). The image works because everyone understands the underlying wisdomâdo not arrive before the judge with a debt you cannot pay. Settle beforehand.

That is excellent advice when the Judge is perfectly just.

The wonder is that the God who sees guilt accurately offers reconciliation before the court convenes. âIt is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgmentâ (Hebrews 9:27). We are still on the way. The offer remains open.

God does not save us by moving the scales.

He saves us by satisfying them.

title: ChatGPT, AI, and the Christian: A Biblical Take on Technology
excerpt: Just like the internet once seemed like a novelty but quickly became indispensable, AI is on a similar trajectory. Itâs time for Christians to begin thinking biblically, wisely, and honestly about this powerful tool.
content:
A Typewriter, AOL, and the Internet

The first paper I ever wrote was on a Remington typewriter. No, Iâm not 100 years oldâIâm 42. I remember the sound of pressing the keys, the piano-like mechanism of a metal lever placing ink on the page, and the satisfying slam of the carriage return marking the accomplishment of one more line of text. And I remember the blessing of using Wite-Out to fix mistakes.

This device was an entire printing press that fit on my desk. It would have made Gutenberg blush, and it was certainly a massive upgrade from having to write long-form cursive in third grade.

Iâve never understood cursive, and I never will. Why? What was the point?

A few years passed, and eventually, a new sound replaced my trusty typewriter. This sound was made possible by a company called America Online (AOL). It sounded something like this:

krrsssshhh, krrsssshhhh, meeewop, meewop.

For those of you too young to remember, the internet used to be delivered to your mailbox on CDs, which you would insert into your desktop computer. These little blessings from AOL granted you free access to THE INTERNET. At first, they offered one hour of free internet, then ten, then fifty. I believe the last CD I received promised 1,000 free hours.

Of course, these free hours were just a clever ploy to get you hookedâAOLâs version of a gateway drugâso that, inevitably, youâd beg your parents for a subscription. But my dad didnât care about the internet; all he knew was that it jammed up the phone line, making it impossible for anyone to call the house. In his words, it was simply âa waste of time.â

That statement always stuck with me. While I agree that you can waste time on the internetâand believe me, I have. Thereâs a reason I know all of the conspiracy theories about the Great Pyramid of Giza. But when I used the internet as a research tool, it didnât waste timeâit drastically saved it. A lot of it. And still does to this day.

The internet changed study, research, and productivity forever. I no longer had to go to the school library and use the Dewey Decimal System to find relevant content in a physical book. I could put my topic into LexisNexis or Dogpile (these were search engines before Google existed), and with the click of a button it would give me the title, chapter, section, and sometimes even the printed page in a digital format.

Just like the internet once seemed like a novelty but quickly became indispensable, AI is on a similar trajectory. Itâs time for Christians to begin thinking biblically, wisely, and honestly about this powerful tool.

AI Is Just a Tool

Said simply, AI is a tool. Itâs no different than a lawn mower. Both were designed for a purpose, and both are morally neutral. The only moral agent with both of these devices is the operator who is using them. Intentional homicide by lawn mower is a real category, and people have used lawn mowers as instruments of death for decades.

Itâs not the intention of this blog to list out all of the different AI tools and how to use them and help you understand what AI isâthere are thousands of videos on YouTube that can give you that information a lot better than I can. In fact, a pastor trying to explain the technical details of AI agents and LLMs is like asking a flight attendant to tell you how to land the plane.

However, my role as a pastor does require me to be knowledgeable of these tools and know how to interact with them so that I can encourage others on how to leverage them for your own edification and, in turn, for the edification of the church. Itâs also my job to warn of the inherent pitfalls of this tool. Thereâs a reason the manual on a lawn mower still has a picture of someone putting their foot under the blade with a giant red circle and a line through it.

For most of you, at the time of this writing, your main use case for AI will be tools like ChatGPT, NotebookLM, Gronk, and the like. It will be you asking a question of these LLMs and getting a response back or asking it to perform a simple task such as:

  • âWrite a blog about AI.â
  • âTell me when Tom Pettyâs birthday is.â
  • âList all the people that appear in the Bible in chronological order.â

I feel that until AI agents become more adopted by lay users, this will be how these platforms will be used for the foreseeable future.

Is there more that can be done? Absolutely. Will most attempt to do that? No.

Where I grew up in Northern Wisconsin there is a thing called a Lawnmower Drag Race at the county fair. These are decked-out lawn mowers with 500-horsepower engines that can do 0â60 in 5 seconds. Will most do the same with theirs to clip their grass? No.

Is it awesome? Yes, yes it is. And if that makes me a hillbillyâ¦ so be it.

But before we talk about how Christians should use AIâor how they shouldnâtâwe need to clarify something foundational: what do we mean by intelligence in the first place?

A Note on Intelligence

We need to define this term and speak to what it is and is not.

Artificial Intelligence (AI)

In AI, intelligence refers to the ability of a machine or algorithm to process information, recognize patterns, learn from data, and make decisions based on statistical probabilities. This intelligence is not conscious, moral, or self-awareâit is a simulation of human problem-solving.

  • AI intelligence is data-driven and relies on algorithms.
  • It lacks wisdom, understanding, or discernmentâit only follows rules and learns from data.
  • It does not possess a soul, emotions, or the ability to seek truth beyond computation.

Biblical Intelligence (Wisdom & Understanding)

The Bible does not simply equate intelligence with knowledge or processing power. Instead, it often links intelligence with wisdom, understanding, and discernment, which come from God.

  • Proverbs 9:10 â âThe fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.â
  • James 3:17 â âBut the wisdom that comes from heaven is first of all pure; then peace-loving, considerate, submissive, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere.â
  • Proverbs 2:6 â âFor the Lord gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding.â

True intelligence is seen as a gift from God, rather than something humans can generate independently.

AI can mimic intelligence, but it lacks true wisdom, understanding, and moral discernmentâthe things that the Bible emphasizes as true intelligence.

Biblical intelligence is relational (connected to God), while AI intelligence is functional (processing data for tasks).

The easiest way to think about this is that AI is from the mind of man; intelligence is from the mind of God.

Key Differences

AspectArtificial Intelligence (AI)Biblical Intelligence
SourceData, algorithms, human programmingGod, fear of the Lord
NaturePattern recognition, learning from dataWisdom, discernment, moral understanding
PurposeProblem-solving, automation, efficiencyRighteousness, truth, and godly living
Moral CapacityNone â follows logic, but has no ethicsTied to morality and righteousness

With that understanding, we need to know that AI will have bias and fallibility and involve a lot of groupthink since it is only compiling data and not truly creating it.

How AI Can Be Helpful for Believers

That said, here are just a few ways that I think AI will be edifying and helpful for the believer.

And again, I need to preface these statements with the truism that nothing can replace inductive Bible studyâthat is, God speaking directly to you through His Word. Itâs one of the highest forms of worship.

It also cannot replace sitting under the preaching of the Word in a local congregation. It cannot replace the gift that God has given to you in having a local pastor bring the Word to you.

AI can give you information, but it cannot pray for you. Itâs not thinking about you on a spiritual level when it responds to your questions. It will never ask you the why behind the why and drill down to the heart of any matter. AI is a toolânot a teacher, and definitely not a pastor.

With this in mind, letâs look at some inputs:

  • Historical Context â Asking ChatGPT to bring you historical context on a given book of the Bible is nothing short of astounding. You can ask continuous drill-down questions such as âWho was the king during this time period?â or âWhat were some of the problems facing this historical context?â
  • Cross References â ChatGPT can deliver reference verses for your further study. âCan you share a reference verse that bolsters the points found in Romans 12:1â2?â
  • Quick Bible Verses â âGive me a few Bible verses to share with someone who is grieving.â
  • Word Studies in Original Languages â âWhat is the biblical Greek word for âslave,â and give me all the uses of it in the New Testament in an organized chart.â
  • Themes of Books â âWhat is the main theme of Obadiah from a Reformed Dispensational position?â
  • Theological Debate â Yes, this is nerdy, but helpful. Prompt: âYou are covenantal in your theology. I am dispensational. We are going to debate the two. You will begin the debate.â
  • Theological Tests â You can ask it to create a 10-question quiz that you would give to a seminary student to see if they understand the Trinity.
  • Apologetics â âWhat are the main verses that a Mormon is going to attack in the New Testament to show that the Bible is not true? Give me 3 arguments for each verse showing that their view is incorrect.â
  • Apologetic Debate â You can have lengthy conversations with ChatGPT to hone your skills. Try: âYou are about to get into a debate with me. You are a member of the FLDS. I am a Reformed Bible-believing Christian. You will lead off the debate. You begin now.â

This is not an exhaustive list by any means, but hopefully gives you an example of what is possible for edification purposes using the tool ChatGPT.

Modest Warnings

Now for the part youâve all been wanting to hear, the warnings. The juicy part where all the luddites get excited to hear Pastor Brett say âAI is the devil and the machines are coming for your kids!â A lot of Christian podcasts have come out lately to hate on AI and chatGPT. Cursing the darkness gets more clicks than being modest. Iâve honestly enjoyed listening to some of them just to simply hear the overstatements that are made.

When the personal computer came out plenty of ink was spilled over if Pastors should be allowed to use them in sermon prep. Donât believe me? Read this.

That was originally written March 1987. Was the computer a cheat-code? Were these pastors losing their integrity because they could type without worrying about grammatical errors? Such suspense!

I love that writerâs perspectiveâ¦because itâs mine as well. The computer is a tool just like chatGPT is a tool.

With that said, here are some modest warnings.

  • You still need to know your Bible. ChatGPT might sound confident, but itâs only as good as the data itâs trained onâand that data includes human errors, theological confusion, and cultural assumptions. If you donât know the Scriptures well, youâre at the mercy of whatever the algorithm gives you. Iâve caught ChatGPT making subtle theological mistakes more than once. But when I pushed back with Scriptureâsaying, âHow does that reconcile with [insert verse]?ââit often admitted the oversight. Thatâs the point: itâs fallible. You must know your Bible, because ChatGPT doesnât love truthâyou do.

  • It is not a Pastor. ChatGPT does not care about you. It doesnât care about your feelings. It doesnât know you personally. Your pastor does. When your pastors give you answers to your questions or preach sermons, they have thought about you on an individual level. They are thinking about your soul, your feelings, and the tone needed to best encourage you. Just this morning I had a brother reach out to me about a sermon series by John MacArthur and he wanted to know if he should listen to it. I told him not to. He struggles with assurance, and MacArthur is too heavy-handed in this area for this brotherâs current state, so I referred him to a book by R.C. Sproul. That is something ChatGPT cannot do. Your Pastors are a gift to you from God.

  • God loves integrity. You can use ChatGPT to respond to emails, write texts, and yesâ¦ write papers and even sermons. However, you will stand before God one day, and He ultimately knows whether you have written something yourself or if you have lied or forged what you claim to be your own. I know you want a lot more on thisâ¦ but thatâs all Iâm going to give you.

  • It can train your heart without you realizing it. Every tool you use shapes you in return. The more you turn to ChatGPT for insight, reflection, or even spiritual guidance, the more you may be tempted to want fast answers, clever responses, and tidy explanations. But thatâs not how God works. The Christian life is slow and intentional. Itâs shaped through prayer, community, repentance, suffering, and meditating on Scriptureânot instant responses from a bot. Guard your heart.

Final Thoughts

AI isnât the enemy. Itâs a tool. A powerful one.

Use it with wisdom. Use it with discernment. But donât let it replace your Bible, your pastor, or the Spiritâs slow work in your life.

And maybeâjust maybeâuse it to write a blog like this. But only if youâre honest about it. (This entire âfinal thoughtsâ section was written by AI. I prompted: âwrite an ending to this blogâ)

title: Genesis 22:1-19
excerpt: Genesis 22:1-19 View this sermon Behold the Lamb (Genesis 22:1-19) The joyous carols and glimmering lights of Christmas often transport us to Bethlehem, where a humble manger cradled the Savior of the world. Yet, toâ¦
content: Genesis 22:1-19 View this sermon Behold the Lamb (Genesis 22:1-19) The joyous carols and glimmering lights of Christmas often transport us to Bethlehem, where a humble manger cradled the Savior of the world. Yet, to truly grasp the magnitude of this event, we might journey further back, to a mountaintop in Moriah. It is here, in the raw narrative of Genesis 22, that we are offered a profound glimpse into the heart of Christmas from the perspective of a Father poised to sacrifice His only Son. Genesis 20-21 chronicles Abrahamâs journey, reflecting our shared human tendencies to waver and stray. Yet, it is in Genesis 22:1-19 where the narrative transforms, echoing a divine resonance. Abrahamâs heart-wrenching ascent to Moriah with Isaac parallels a divine foreshadowing of what the Heavenly Father would endure for the sake of humanity. Behold the sacrifice Genesis 22:1-2 The winding faith journey of Abraham in Genesis reveals a tableau of divine promises interwoven with profound tests. As we delve into Genesis 22, we are confronted with a test that is nothing short of scandalous. âAfter these things God tested Abrahamâ¦â The narrative, following the affirmations and promises of Genesis 12:7, 13:14-16, 15:1-6, and 17:15-19, now presents an instruction that must have struck Abraham like a cold slap in the face. Here, Godâs voice doesnât simply call; it demands, âAbraham!â His reply, immediate and attentive, âHere I am,â soon gives way to an unfathomable request. âTake your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offeringâ¦â Every word in this directive carries a profound weight. Your son. Your only son. Whom you love. The depth of the sacrifice being asked is jarring, even horrifying. This is the very son through whom the covenantal promises were to be realized. The starkness of this command is meant to scandalize the reader. How could a loving God ask for such a heart-wrenching sacrifice? It is this very scandal that captures the essence of sacrifice and faith. And while Abrahamâs pain and confusion are palpable, a foreshadowing emerges from the shadows of this event. As the narrative unfolds, we come to a divine revelation: God Himself would face a similar choice. Only in His case, there would be no ram in the thicket, no last-minute reprieve. God would carry through with the ultimate sacrifice, offering His only Son for the redemption of humanity. In the scandal of Moriah, we are led to confront the enormity of Calvary. The visceral reaction we have to Abrahamâs test is a mere glimpse of the heart-wrenching decision the Father made. By juxtaposing these events, we gain a deeper appreciation for the boundless love of God, who did what He spared Abraham from doing. The true cost of such love is both scandalous and salvific, inviting us to behold the sacrifice with renewed awe and gratitude. Behold the obedience Genesis 22:3-6 The narrative that unfurls in Genesis 22 is not merely a historical account; it is a layered tapestry of faith, obedience, and foreshadowing. Each step Abraham takes echoes with profound implications, not just for him, but for the Savior to come. âSo Abraham rose early in the morningâ¦â With the dawning of a new day, Abrahamâs immediate response captures his unwavering resolve to heed Godâs daunting call. Each detail of his preparation, from saddling his donkey to cutting the wood, is tinged with the weight of sacrifice and surrender. Yet, amidst the familiar narrative emerges a poignant detail: Isaac, often depicted as a mere child in popular retellings, would have been an adult at this time. His presence is not that of an unsuspecting child, but of a willing participant. Carrying the wood for his own sacrifice, Isaacâs actions mirror a deep-seated obedience akin to his fatherâs. This image of a son bearing the weight of wood up a hill cannot be overlooked, for it is a haunting prelude to another Son, Christ, who would willingly bear the wood of the cross centuries later. On the third day, Moriahâs silhouette beckons in the distance, an emblem of the impending sacrifice. The significance of the âthird dayâ is deeply entrenched in biblical symbolism, foreshadowing the pivotal third day of Christâs resurrection. Abrahamâs profound words to his servants, âI and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you,â not only underscore the act of obedience as worship, as echoed in Romans 12:1, but also set the stage for the greatest act of worship. The obedience of Christ. Verse 6 offers a further reflection of this parallel. As Abraham places the weight of the sacrificial wood upon Isaac, one is reminded of the cross Christ bore willingly. Their journey itselfâfather and son, ascending Moriah togetherâis a testament to obedience, faith, and foretelling. Behold the provision Genesis 22:7-14 Isaac, in his innocent yet perceptive observation, poses a question that echoes through time, âBehold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?â The weight of this query, posed by a son bearing the wood of his own intended sacrifice, is staggering. In this question, one can feel the very heartbeat of humanityâs quest for understanding, for a sense of Godâs redemptive plan. Abrahamâs response, spoken with a faith that pierces the annals of history, declares, âGod will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.â Here, Abrahamâs faith and prophetic insight merge. He speaks of a lamb, yet the narrative takes a turn. Upon reaching the designated place, it isnât a lamb that God provides, but a ram caught in a thicket. While the ram serves as an immediate substitute for Isaac, itâs the absent lamb that captures our attention. The lamb, the true sacrificial offering, wouldnât be found on Moriah that day. The meticulous details of Abraham preparing the altar, arranging the wood, and the disquieting act of binding his son all culminate to a moment that is suddenly halted by a divine intervention. The angel of the LORD intervenes just as the knife was poised, a testament to the Lordâs omniscient timing and His insurmountable mercy. But herein lies the profound prophetic mystery. While Abraham proclaimed the provision of a lamb, it was a ram that was caught and subsequently offered. This divinely orchestrated substitution points forward to an event of monumental significance. Thousands of years later, on that very mount, God would provide not a ram, but finally, the LambâChrist Jesus, the ultimate and perfect sacrifice for humanityâs sins. This passage culminates with Abrahamâs declaration: âThe LORD will provide.â A statement of unwavering faith that echoes even now, reminding us of Godâs providence and His masterful tapestry of redemption. As we ponder this narrative, the writer of Hebrews offers a reflection on Abrahamâs faith in Hebrews 11:17-19, emphasizing that, with God, all things are indeed possible. Behold the blessingâ¦of Christmas Genesis 22:15-19 Upon reading Genesis 22, our initial emotions are punctuated by shock and unease. How could a loving God ask a father to sacrifice his beloved son? The gravity of such a command is unsettling, to say the least. However, as the narrative unfolds, the profound significance of this chapter becomes evident. Itâs not just a story of Abrahamâs faith, but a mirror reflecting the vastness of Godâs sacrificial love for humanity. The angel of the LORDâs proclamation from heaven rings with divine resolve. The words, âBecause you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son,â bear weight. They simultaneously allude to Abrahamâs obedience and forecast the heart-wrenching sacrifice God Himself was willing to make for us. The promise to Abrahamâs âoffspringââsingularly referencing Christ in Galatians 3:16â underscores the global blessing and salvation planned through Jesus. title: Genesis 20:1-21:34
excerpt: Genesis 20:1-21:34 View this sermon Still faithful (Genesis 20:1-21:34 ) Throughout the annals of human history, a recurring theme surfaces: our constant unfaithfulness. We, as a collective, have displayed a propensityâ¦
content: Genesis 20:1-21:34 View this sermon Still faithful (Genesis 20:1-21:34 ) Throughout the annals of human history, a recurring theme surfaces: our constant unfaithfulness. We, as a collective, have displayed a propensity to waver, to doubt, and to stray. Yet, there is an enduring and unyielding truth that confronts our shortcomingsâGodâs unwavering faithfulness. This profound testament finds its roots in the foundational narratives of Genesis. As we traverse the chapters of Genesis 20-21, we encounter Abraham, a figure who, despite his stature, is not immune to human frailty. He falters, complicates matters, and at times, outright fails. However, juxtaposed against Abrahamâs actions is Godâs steadfast character. He consistently blesses amidst our missteps, offers compassion when we ensnare ourselves in complexities, and maintains an unwavering faithfulness even when we falter. The birth of Isaac in these passages is not just the fulfillment of a promise, but a powerful testament to grace. It reminds us, echoing the words of Romans 5:20-21, that âwhere sin increased, grace abounded all the more.â In other words, Isaacâs birth reminds us that you cannot out-sin grace. When you backslideâ¦again Genesis 20:1-18 Biblical narratives often unveil surprising facets of human nature juxtaposed against the incomprehensible grace and justice of God. Genesis 20 stands as a testament to this paradox, revealing the flaws even within great patriarchs like Abraham, and more shockingly, Godâs surprising favor towards them despite their failings. Abraham, on his journey through Gerar, revisits an old tactic from Genesis 12:10-20, by introducing Sarah as his sister out of fear. This isnât just a minor deception; it jeopardizes the sanctity of marital bonds and places others in moral jeopardy. Abimelech, the king of Gerar, becomes an unsuspecting player in this charade, taking Sarah based on this lie. One would expect Abraham to bear the consequences of his actions. Yet, in a twist, it is Abimelech who receives a divine warning, facing repercussions for a sin he unknowingly committed. Here lies the profound mystery of Godâs grace and justice: despite Abrahamâs glaring fault, God upholds His covenant, protecting Sarah from dishonor and Abraham from potential harm. Abimelechâs response showcases a deep-seated integrity. Upon realizing the truth, he not only restores Sarah to Abraham but blesses him with gifts, displaying righteousness and grace even in the face of deception. Somehow, it is not Abimelech who is blessed but Abraham, the one who caused the trouble in the first place. The shocking irony is Abrahamâs intercession, leading to Godâs healing touch upon Abimelechâs household. Why does Abraham, our revered patriarch, repeatedly falter in this manner? Paulâs reflections in Romans 7:15-8:1 shed light on this conundrum, highlighting the tug-of-war between our intentions and actions. However, the overarching message of this chapter remains the perplexing depth of Godâs grace. Even when we are clearly in the wrong, Godâs promise of grace endures. This isnât an endorsement of our missteps, but a powerful testament to Godâs unwavering commitment to His promises. In our recurrent shortcomings, this story reminds us of the boundless grace that God bestows, the shocking unmerited and, yes, unfair blessing of grace. He still blesses Genesis 21:1-7 Genesis 20 and 21, when read in succession, emerge as profound chapters that intricately interweave human flaws with Godâs ageless grace. They present a narrative continuum, from Abrahamâs repeated transgressions to the fulfillment of a long-awaited promise, they highlight Godâs predestined blessings even amidst human unfaithfulness. In Genesis 20, Abrahamâs doubt is evident as he introduces Sarah as his sister, risking Godâs promise for a second time. The ripple effect of his actions is swift and impacts the unsuspecting Abimelech. Yet, in a turn of events, Abraham, the very orchestrator of the deceit, becomes the vessel of intercession for the restoration of Abimelechâs household. The irony is profound: as Abraham himself had grappled with the prolonged barrenness of his wife, Sarah, and the delay of Godâs promise, so Abimelechâs house experiences a momentary barrenness due to Abrahamâs actions. However, as we transition into Genesis 21, the landscape dramatically changes. Sarah, against all worldly odds, conceives and gives birth to Isaac. The prayers Abraham once sent up, laden with impatience and doubt, are finally answered. This isnât just an answer to prayer; itâs a manifestation of Godâs unmerited favor. This grace was not a reaction to Abrahamâs faithfulness, but was set into motion even before his birth. Ephesians 1:3-19 echoes this sentiment powerfully. It speaks of blessings that were preordained, chosen and destined for us before the worldâs foundation. This is unmerited grace in its purest form. Sarahâs laughter, once a skeptical response, evolves into an emblem of joy and wonder at Godâs undying faithfulness. The juxtaposition of Abrahamâs actions in Genesis 20 with the blessings in Genesis 21 is both a reflection of Godâs patience and His eternal plans, which are rooted in grace, not human merit. While our journey may be punctuated with backsliding moments, Godâs roadmap for us, etched before our very existence, ensures that His blessings and grace will always find their way to us. This, then, is the crux of these chapters: A testament to a divine love and preplanned grace that remain unyielding amidst our human frailties. When you complicate thingsâ¦again Genesis 21:8-11 The celebratory atmosphere surrounding Isaacâs weaning is a poignant reminder of Godâs faithfulness. Yet, while this should have been an unadulterated moment of joy in response to Godâs grace, especially following the problematic events in Gerar, shadows from Abrahamâs past decisions cast their shade. Sarah observes Ishmael laughing, a laughter tinged with mockery. The same child, born out of an earlier attempt to hasten Godâs promise, now becomes a point of contention. Sarahâs demand for Hagar and Ishmaelâs exile draws a clear line of demarcation between Isaac, the child of promise, and Ishmael, the child of human impatience. While the decision might align with the cultural norms of the time, as seen in Genesis 25:5-6, the emotional weight it carries is undeniable. Abrahamâs displeasure, an echo of his previous transgressions, stands out. The patriarch, who once deceived out of fear and attempted to expedite Godâs promise, now faces the ramifications of those decisions at a time when he should have been purely rejoicing. Reflecting on Genesis 16:1-6, the root of this complication becomes evident. Abraham and Sarahâs choice to bring Hagar into their narrative was an attempt to simplify Godâs promise, to find a quick solution. But as weâve seen from Genesis 20 onward, human attempts to shortcut divine plans often lead to more intricate problems. He still has compassion Genesis 21:12-21 In the evolving narrative from Genesis 20 to 21:21, a pattern emergesâhuman choices consistently entangle, but Godâs grace gracefully disentangles. Starting with Abrahamâs deception, then the birth of Isaac, and the familial tensions with Hagar and Ishmael, we witness a series of imperfect decisions followed by Godâs perfect interventions. And now, in the throes of a painful decision to separate Ishmael from Isaac, Godâs voice of compassion rises above all else. Godâs directives to Abraham in Genesis 21:12-13 reiterate His purpose and plans. He assures Abraham of His intention for Isaac, anchoring him to the initial promise, and then, beautifully, he does not dismiss Ishmaelâs fate. The words, âAnd I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also, because he is your offspring,â are a testament to Godâs undiscriminating love. Even as the child, a product of human impatience, is cast aside, God remains committed to His promise made in Genesis 17:20-21. As Hagar, burd

title: Genesis 19:1-38
excerpt: Genesis 19:1-38 View this sermon Descent into Sodom (Genesis 19:1-38) In John 17:9-19, Jesus starkly differentiates between the world and His followers, a distinction that prompts us to ponder: what does it look like toâ¦
content: Genesis 19:1-38 View this sermon Descent into Sodom (Genesis 19:1-38) In John 17:9-19, Jesus starkly differentiates between the world and His followers, a distinction that prompts us to ponder: what does it look like to be a friend of the world? James 4:4 provides an unsettling clarity to this query, warning us that friendship with the world makes us enemies of God. This profound divergence in relationship is vividly illustrated in the juxtaposition of Abraham and Lotâs stories in Genesis 18 and 19. Abrahamâs profound communion with God in Genesis 18 stands in stark and alarming contrast to Lotâs entanglements with worldly concerns in Genesis 19. Luke 9:23-25 further deepens this narrative, emphasizing the cost of discipleship and prompting us to consider the true worth of worldly gains if they come at the soulâs expense. Delving into Genesis 19, we witness Lotâs strained hospitality towards the angels, reflecting his struggle against Sodomâs worldly influences. The ensuing moral degradation of Sodomâs residents overshadows Lotâs voice of reason, emphasizing the debilitating consequences of worldliness. Lotâs futile attempt to caution his sons-in-law further underscores his eroded impact, a byproduct of his compromised stand in Sodom. The narrative takes a chilling turn as the angels warn Lot, and yet, both he and his wife falter, revealing the peril of being ensnared by worldly allure. As Sodom and Gomorrah burn, Lotâs subsequent actions and those of his daughters bear testament to the ultimate desolation wrought by worldlinessâa loss of hope and a descent into moral decay. What will it profit you to gain the world Genesis 19:1-3 Genesis 19:1-3 paints a picture thatâs both compelling and cautionary. Weâre reintroduced to Lot, once a wanderer in tandem with his uncle Abraham, now positioned at the pivotal gateway of Sodom. This isnât a fleeting visit; itâs a deliberate placement, a culmination of decisions. From initially choosing to live near sin in Genesis 13:1-13, to progressively immersing himself within its walls in Genesis 14:12, by Genesis 19:1 Lot is not merely a resident, but appears to be a prominent figure in Sodom. As the narrative unfolds with the angelsâ visit, we canât help but draw parallels between Lotâs and Abrahamâs encounters. Both exhibit hospitality, but the stark difference lies in the depth and nature of their offerings. Abraham, though materially wealthy, never lost sight of his divine purpose, resulting in a heartfelt and lavish welcome for his guests. In contrast, Lotâs offerings, particularly the unleavened bread which implies hasty preparations, seem almost perfunctory, hinting at the subtle compromises heâs made living amidst Sodomâs influences. Further, Lotâs insistence on the angels staying with him, while showcasing a remnant of his righteousness, also underscores a deeper truth: heâs aware of the cityâs perils, a far cry from the open tents of Abraham. The narrative prompts us to consider the age-old question, âWhat will it profit you to gain the world?â Lot, with his position and prominence in Sodom, seems to have gained the world, so to speak. But is he truly better off than Abraham? As we juxtapose the two, it becomes evident that while Lot might have worldly stature, he seems to have traded away the profound spiritual intimacy and clarity that Abraham enjoyed. In gaining Sodom, Lot seems to have lost something far more valuable, which is seen in the next sections. â¦and lose your voice Genesis 19:4-11 Genesis 19:4-11 presents a disturbing scene that magnifies the severe degradation of Sodomâs societal values, a theme vividly illustrated through various biblical references. The entirety of the cityâs men, both young and old, surround Lotâs home with a sinister intent that is far from innocent curiosity. Their actions reflect a society that has not only strayed from the righteous path, but has also actively embraced its opposition to God. This societal decay resonates powerfully with Paulâs discourse in Romans 1:18-32. Paul describes a society that has willingly turned its back on God, resulting in Him âgiving them upâ to their debased minds and desires. The explicit mention of homosexual acts in Romans, and its link to Sodomâs aggressive mob, serves as a stark warning. It illustrates the extent of a societyâs downfall when it not only indulges in such acts, but also celebrates them. This isnât merely about individual choices; itâs about a collective abandonment of divine guidance, leading to societal chaos. Moreover, the audacity with which the men of Sodom challenge Lot, saying, âhe has become the judge,â underscores their brazen disregard for moral standards. This echoes the sentiment from Romans 2:1-5, wherein individuals, despite being deeply flawed, are quick to pass judgment. Lotâs compromised stance, offering his daughters in place of his guests, further emphasizes this relative morality. Itâs a bleak picture: even the voice that seeks to mediate or negotiate is itself mired in compromise. This entire scenario paints the chilling picture of a society thatâs not merely lost, but is actively under the wrath of God. Itâs a society where the customary norms of right and wrong are obliterated, where even a whisper of righteousness is drowned in a cacophony of wickedness. Itâs not just about the manifestation of specific sins, but the collective celebration of them, an alarming reminder of the potential depth of human depravity when society distances itself from divine truth. In such a scenario, weâre compelled to ponder: what profit is there in gaining a world like that? For in the process of embracing and amplifying such wickedness, society, including those who might have once stood against it, lose their voice. The passage is about more than Sodom, however. Itâs a grim portrayal of a man that, in his quest for unchecked freedoms and worldly gains, has sacrificed the very moral compass that once directed his path. The narrative stands as a solemn reminder: gaining the world at the cost of our moral voice is a hollow victory, one fraught with profound loss and regret. â¦and lose your impact Genesis 19:12-14 Genesis 19:12-14 offers an unsettling prelude to Sodomâs impending annihilation, illuminating a crucial message on the ephemeral nature of worldly gains and the true essence of enduring influence. The question posed to the reader is stark and poignant: what value do material achievements hold if one loses their impact, particularly on those closest to them? As the divine messengers unveil the imminent destruction to Lot, their urgency to save his family underscores the gravitas of the situation. Yet, itâs Lotâs desperate plea to his sons-in-law that brings the narrativeâs true tragedy to the forefront. Despite his earnest warnings, they dismiss him, viewing his proclamations as nothing more than playful jest. This disheartening response reveals the extent to which Lotâs influence has waned, even among his immediate family. Paulâs words in 1 Corinthians 3:10-15 are particularly illuminating in understanding this predicament. Paul speaks of building oneâs life on a foundation, with Christ being the only true and lasting cornerstone. However, the materials one choosesâgold, silver, precious stones, or wood, hay, and strawâdetermine the endurance and worth of oneâs life work. As the âDayâ of judgment approaches, the true quality of each personâs work becomes evident. While some works endure the purifying fire, symbolizing eternal rewards, others are consumed, indicating a life of transient pursuits. In Lotâs context, his life in Sodom, possibly characterized by compromise and alignment with the cityâs fleeting values, seems to have rendered his voice ineffective at a pivotal moment. Though he might be âsaved through fireâ (1 Cor 3:15), reflecting a salvation from immediate destruction, the potential loss of his family signifies a deeper tragedy.
