This suggests several matters: the Bible will not contradict itself; the Scriptures are coherent and consistent. The Bible, being a divine book, has mystery. It must be recognized that the Bible contains many things that are hard to understand. Bible students must acknowledge that they cannot always ascertain what a given passage means. The Bible is mysterious in four areas: inerrancy, prophecy, miracles, and difficult doctrines such as the Trinity.â I once was in attendance at a seminar given by Norman Geisler. In response to a question on the reliability of the doctrine of inerrancy, Geisler asked the person, âDo you believe in God?â The person replied in the affirmative. âDo you believe He is perfect?â Again the person said âyes.â âDo you believe He wrote the Bible?â was the next question Geisler posed. Once more the person enthusiastically answered affirmatively. Geisler smiled and said, âYou have your answer.â Some may consider Geislerâs approach simplistic or evasive, but I do not. I submit this logic is biblical and therefore quite sound and convincing. The theologian R. C. Sproul wrote the Foreword for John MacArthurâs book The Inerrant Word and in it penned these trenchant words: âThe Bible is the Word of God, which errs.â From the advent of neoorthodox theology in the early twentieth century, this assertion has become a mantra among those who want to have a high view of Scripture while avoiding the academic liability of asserting biblical infallibility and inerrancy. But this statement represents the classic case of having oneâs cake and eating it too. It is the quintessential oxymoron. Let us look again at this untenable theological formula. If we eliminate the first part, âThe Bible isâ we get âThe Word of God, which errs.â If we parse it further and scratch out âthe Word ofâ and âwhich,â we reach the bottom line: âGod errs.â The idea that God errs in any way, in any place, or on any endeavor is repugnant to the mind as well as the soul. Here, biblical criticism reaches the nadir of biblical vandalism. How could any sentient creature conceive of a formula that speaks of the Word of God as errant? Also at the onset, and as was included in the last weekâs study, it is important to state that the words âinerrancyâ or âinfallibilityâ (synonymous terms meaning the same thing), âinspiration,â and âillumination,â as well as the authority implicit in each, must be understood as relating to Scripture only in its original languages, and neither to ancient copies nor modern translations. After concluding a section on inspiration is his classic work on biblical interpretation, Living by the Book , in which he wrote, âThe text of the Bible is not the musing of men but a supernatural product, the very Word of God,â Howard Hendricks stated several uncompromising facts regarding inerrancy. Hendricks said, âIn order to be authoritative, the Bible must be true, that is, without error.â A Bible that is not trustworthy is nothing more than another history book, one that has no special hold on our lives. From the same paragraph in Hendricksâ book, these unambiguous and provocative words: âEither the Bible is without error in all, or it is not without error at all.â I believe these words should cause us all to pause and consider: do we really believe the Bible we hold in our hands is the inerrant Word of God, exercising authority over our lives in practically every meaningful mater, having supernatural power to guide and even judge us as if God Himself was speaking to us, or do we not? As Hendricks points out, there is no middle ground. âA partially inerrant Bible is an errant Bible.â âThe Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy,â a noteworthy and very influential document on the doctrine of inerrancy, formulated in 1978 by a group of conservative theologians and church leaders, and signed by the likes of Geisler, MacArthur, Piper, and Sproul, is something every Christian should read carefully and think through. Because this document is so thorough and forceful, Pastors Matt and Paul have it permanently on the Barabbas Rd. website. Below is a summary excerpt: God, who is Himself Truth and speaks truth only, has inspired Holy Scripture in order thereby to reveal Himself to lost mankind through Jesus Christ as Creator and Lord, Redeemer and Judge. Holy Scripture is Godâs witness to Himself. Holy Scripture, being Godâs own Word, written by men prepared and superintended by His Spirit, is of infallible divine authority in all matters upon which it touches: it is to be believed, as Godâs instruction, in all that it affirms, obeyed, as Godâs command, in all that it requires; embraced, as Godâs pledge, in all that it promises. The Holy Spirit, Scriptureâs divine Author, both authenticates it to us by His inward witness and opens our minds to understand its meaning. Being wholly and verbally God-given, Scripture is without error or fault in all its teaching, no less in what it states about Godâs acts in creation, about the events of world history, and about its own literary origins under God, than in its witness to Godâs saving grace in individual lives. The authority of Scripture is inescapably impaired if this total divine inerrancy is in any way limited or disregarded, or made relative to a view of truth contrary to the Bibleâs own; and such lapses bring serious loss to both the individual and the Church. Although it is true, as has been stated above and in last weekâs blog on inspiration, that defending the authenticity and authority of the Scriptures is not without problems, these human errors are surprisingly few. title: Inspiration
excerpt: Inspiration This and the following blog on inerrancy will be writings in defense of the Word of God as being both inspired and inerrant. This weekâs study (even though it is abbreviated, it is a little longer thanâ¦
content: Inspiration This and the following blog on inerrancy will be writings in defense of the Word of God as being both inspired and inerrant. This weekâs study (even though it is abbreviated, it is a little longer than usual; I hope you will hang with me) will focus on the doctrine of inspiration. âDoctrineâ comes from the Latin doctrina , meaning teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge . Recognizing that âdoctrineâ has a wide semantical range (i.e., there are many synonymous terms), and some may argue that âbeliefâ would be a better choice, I feel confident in saying most all Christians would agree biblically speaking, âdoctrineâ means truth. It should be understood at the start that I am not putting forth a theory of my own; far from it. Rather, I am defending a doctrine of the Bible. Inspiration is not what I say; inspiration is what God said in the Bible: ESV 2 Timothy 3:16 All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, Please note the opening words, âall Scripture.â In spite of the direct clarity of these words, people, pastors and teachers, and even renowned scholars persist in claiming that the human writers of the sixty-six books of the Bible were also inspired. Such a position is regrettably wrong and misleading. Certainly, it must be recognized that it is not incorrect to say that the Bible was written by both God and man, so long as it is clear that ââdual authorshipâ presupposes God wrote the Bible through human authors, using their personalities and backgrounds as they suited His purposes. Second Timothy 3:16 and the other verses included in this writing unequivocally proclaim that âall Scripture,â and not the human authors, was inspired âby God.â NLT 2 Timothy 3:16 All Scripture is inspired by God and is useful to teach us what is true and to make us realize what is wrong in our lives. It corrects us when we are wrong and teaches us to do what is right. âThe Bible is the Word of God in such a way that when the Bible speaks, Good speaks.â âB.B. Warfield Many would therefore ask what the problem is? If God said it, doesnât that settle it? But, as incredible and, some may say, arrogant as it may sound, more than a few people, including professing Christians, do not accept this truth. Many liberals believe that the Bible is not the Word of God but only contains the Word of God. Not only is this speculative, but it begs the question who then decides which words are inspired and which are not? Whenever the words of Scripture are ignored, twisted, or undervalued, the supernatural power they contain is diminished. âInspirationâ obviously must be defined. Biblical inspiration is different than the way the word is often used in society today, usually to refer to something of surpassing excellence. âInspirationâ comes from the Greek word Î¸Îµá½¹ÏÎ½ÎµÏÏÏÎ¿Ï ( thee-ah-pe-neus-tos ), which literally means God- breathed . Interestingly, this special word only appears this once in all of the New Testament. In our English dictionaries, âinspiration,â when it refers to respiration, is defined as in-breathing, the act of inhaling, but the Greek word in context carries the opposite meaning: out-breathing. The Scriptures were not breathed in by God, they were breathed out. Friberg, the writer of an outstanding Greek lexicon, defines Î¸Îµá½¹ÏÎ½ÎµÏÏÏÎ¿Ï as pertaining to âcommunication that has been ordained by Godâs authority and produced by the enabling of his Spirit; strictly God-breathed ; hence divinely inspired, inspired by God .â A good inclusive theological definition of inspiration is the following by Zuck ( Biblical Interpretation ): âInspirationâ¦ is the supernatural work of the Holy Spirit whereby He guided and superintended the writers of Scripture so that what they wrote is the word of God. This breathing into the writings, or superintending over the writings, was an act both verbal and plenary. It was verbal in that the Holy Spirit guided in the choice of words, which cannot be separated from thoughts. The Bibleâs inspiration was also plenary in that it extended to every portion of the Bible. As a result it is infallible in truth and final in authority.â¦ Because of its divine origin and nature, the Bible in its original writings was without error.â Next week we will look at the logical consequence of inspiration: inerrancy. Chafer rightly states in his Systematic Theology , âRegarding the Scriptures and plenary, verbal inspiration, it may be said that no other explanation has been the belief of the church from the beginning.â¦ No progress has ever been made in formulating doctrine from the Bible when men have doubted the inspiration of the Scriptures in all its parts.â âRevelationâ is another word that must be understood in this discussion of inspiration. I again quote from Zuck: âThe Bible is revelation (not only a record of revelation), and inspiration is the act whereby God put the revealed truths into infallible written form. Revelation is the communication of truth which would not otherwise be known, whereas inspiration is the process whereby this information is presented accurately in written languagesâ (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek â TAR). It is by inspiration, as Chafer notes, that revelation finds infallible expression. One more key word is âillumination.â Illumination has to do with the work of the Holy Spirit. It could rightly be said that inspiration, revelation, and illumination all are works of the Holy Spirit. Thomas writes in Evangelical Hermeneutics concerning illumination, âDivine revelation and inspiration lie behind the writings of Scripture, and divine illumination functions in connection with manâs ability to understand what is written.â Every Christian should be aware that in a single short passage, all three of these important theological words are found and distinguished from one another (parentheses added below): ESV 1 Corinthians 2:9-13 But, as it is written, âWhat no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love himââ 10 these things God has revealed ( revelation ) to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. 11 For who knows a personâs thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. 12 Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand ( illumination ) the things freely given us by God. 13 And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit ( inspiration ), interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual. Of the three Persons of the Trinity, it is the third Person, the Holy Spirit, who most rightly should be seen as the author of Scripture. That Scripture did not originate with men, but with God is again unmistakably shown form another verse, 2 Peter 1:21 where he Holy Spirit is identified the divine Agent of prophecy. This strategic verse, a corollary or counterpart to 2 Timothy 3:16, underscores the human reception only of divine inspiration: ESV 2 Peter 1:21 For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. Yet, this verse also supports the legitimacy of âdual authorship.â Man did indeed play a crucial role in the transmission of revelation, though not as its originator. While it is, as noted above, incorrect to hold that the human authors were inspired, 1 Peter 1:21 shows that they were moved or borne along by the Holy Spirt, as a ship might be by the wind (âcarried alongâ is the Greek word Ïá½³ÏÏ ( fe-ro ), which the BDAG lexicon contextually defines, âto cause to follow a certain course in direction or conduct, move out of position, drive, the pass-( ive â TAR) can be variously rendered: be moved, be driven, let oneself be moved .â With 2 Peter 1:21 in mind, a brief discussion of a question regularly posed b

title: sixth hour
excerpt: sixth hour Pastor Matt mentioned in his sermon Sunday âThe Sixth Hour,â explaining that while he would have liked to have been able to go into the subject in greater detail than he did, time would not allow. You mayâ¦
content: sixth hour Pastor Matt mentioned in his sermon Sunday âThe Sixth Hour,â explaining that while he would have liked to have been able to go into the subject in greater detail than he did, time would not allow. You may have also heard him say that he had asked me to write this weekâs blog to kind of make up for the understandable shortcoming. Following is my study on John 19:14 and âThe Sixth Hour.â NAS John 19:14 Now it was the day of preparation for the Passover; it was about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jews, âBehold, your King!â The excellent note from the NET (New English Translation) Bible is helpful in providing information about âthe day of preparationâ: The term day of preparationt (ÏÎ±ÏÎ±ÏÎºÎµÏá½µ, paraskeue Ã ) appears in all the gospels as a description of the day on which Jesus died. It could refer to any Friday as the day of preparation for the Sabbath (Saturday), and this is the way the synoptic gospels use the term (Matt 27:62, Mark 15:42, and Luke 23:54). John, however, specifies in addition that this was not only the day of preparation of the Sabbath, but also the day of preparation of the Passover, so that the Sabbath on the following day was the Passover (cf. 19:31). The term day of preparationt (ÏÎ±ÏÎ±ÏÎºÎµÏá½µ, paraskeueÃ) appears in all the gospels as a description of the day on which Jesus died. It could refer to any Friday as the day of preparation for the Sabbath (Saturday), and this is the way the synoptic gospels use the term (Matt 27:62, Mark 15:42, and Luke 23:54). John, however, specifies in addition that this was not only the day of preparation of the Sabbath, but also the day of preparation of the Passover, so that the Sabbath on the following day was the Passover (cf. 19:31). Here are the verses mentioned above NAS Matthew 27:62 Now on the next day, which is the one after the preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered together with Pilate, NAS Mark 15:42 And when evening had already come, because it was the preparation day, that is, the day before the Sabbath, NAS Luke 23:54 And it was the preparation day, and the Sabbath was about to begin. NAS John 19:31 The Jews therefore, because it was the day of preparation, so that the bodies should not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day ), asked Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away. The first thing I would like to say here at the start is that the question of the âsixth hourâ is far from being easily answered. The main reason for this difficulty has to do with the complexities and uncertainties involved in attempting to determine exact times in the New Testament. Notice the text itself says âit was about the sixth hour,â not that it precisely was the sixth hour. John MacArthur offers a comprehensive paragraph from his commentary on Johnâs gospel that sheds light on this reality: The time âwas about the sixth hourâ; or late morning, approaching noon. This statement presents an apparent difficulty, because according to Markâs account (see immediately below â TAR [Thomas A. Rohm]), Jesus was crucified at the third hour (9:00A.M.). But as Andres Kostenberger (whose commentary on Johnâs gospel is certainly among the best and most insightful â TAR) writes, âSince people related the estimated time to the closest three-hour mark, any time between 9:00 A.M. and noon may have led one person to say an event occurred at the third (9:00 A.M.) or the sixth hour (12:00 noon).â D.A. Carson (another top commentator on Johnâs gospel â TAR) cautions against âinsisting on a degree of precision in both Mark and John which, in days before watches, could not have been achieved.â NAS Mark 15:25 And it was the third hour when they crucified Him. Not only would this reference to time have been most probably approximate, but could also be referring to only the beginning of the process, sometime before Jesus was even lifted on the cross. In noting the first instance in Johnâs gospel where time is mentioned, 1:39, Kostenberger offers this germane information on how the ancients viewed time: âThe preponderance of evidence suggests that in the first century of Jesusâ Palestine, time was counted from sunrise to sunset(i.e., from about 6 A.M. until about 6 P.M.; cf. John 11:9). Moreover, the day was divided into three-hour intervals, with people approximating the estimated time to the next full three-hour segment.â When most people read âthe sixth hourâ in John and âthe third hourâ in Mark, it is probably fair to say that their first reaction is negative: âHey, whatâs going on here?â âThis is nothing less than an example of a contradiction in the Bible!â If these people had a couple of relatively inexpensive, elementary resources, Bible dictionary and a single volume commentary, they could learn that seeming problems in the Bible are not contradictions but simply differences. In the case of âthe sixth hourâ and âthe third hour,â they would find that two gospel writers are almost certainly making different points about the same event for purposes particular to their gospels. At Southern California Seminary I have been teaching the gospel of John for nine consecutive years, one to two chapters each year. Iâm just finishing chapter 12 this month. During the first class of each course I illustrate how and why the gospels can differ. I do this by bringing a bag of quilting squares; you know, little three-to-four inch squares of colorful cloth normally used to make quilts with. I have previously selected four stacks â one for each of the gospels â of the same multi-colored squares, about a dozen different patterns, and I spread the stacks out beside one another on a table, and I say, âLetâs say the yellow swatch is the birth of Jesus, the blue striped square is for Jesusâ baptism, the red diamond-patterned one for the feeding of the five-thousand, the black one for the crucifixion, etc. I say for my students to imagine each gospel writer had access to the same pile of squares but arranged them differently and used different colored thread to sew them together according to each writerâs purpose. Most of the same quilting squares are included in each writerâs âquilt,â but some squares are left out of some writerâs âquilt.â John, for example, doesnât have the yellow one; not because the yellow one isnât pretty or important, but simply because it doesnât fit the pattern John is constructing. Matthew, Mark, and Luke do not have the orange polka-dot squares that stand for the Upper Room Discourse that John has, because their purposes are different than Johnâs. Well, I think you get the point. Iâm simplifying, sure, but the point is valid. Each writerâs quilt is made from essentially the same squares and generally look the same, but each is different. Another important relevant point to keep in mind when evaluating so-called âproblemsâ with the biblical text is that we are simply not going to be able always to give satisfactory answers for each question that may arise. I sometimes pose blunt and provocative questions to my students when the occasion arises, such as, âWho are you that you think God owes you a clear, satisfying answer for each question your suspicious mind comes up with?â Surely we are to ask questions of the text, and certainly an inquisitive mind can lead to valuable comprehension. I for one thrive on this dimension of my relationship with God. But oftentimes ceaseless questions posing as a sincere desire to learn more about God, can in reality be a subterfuge masking doubt or disbelief. Arthur W. Pink, the great Reformed theologian of past years who wrote a memorable expansive commentary on the gospel of John, was quite dogmatic in his position on John 19:14. He strongly believed that an in-depth study of the verse that included research into the Jewish customs of the day clearly revealed there was no substantial problem in reconciling the gospel writersâ differing accounts. content: ascension This is a wonderful study, an important study, even a miraculous study: âThe Ascension of Jesus Christââ¦ Although the ascension did not occur until seven weeks after the resurrection, I have taken the liberty in including it as a conclusion to the four-part Easter series I Hope you have been following: âLamb Selection Day,â âCrucifixion,â Resurrection,â and now âAscension.â Most people know a lot about the crucifixion and the resurrection, but it has been my observation that not near as many people know about the ascension. âThe ascensionâ is the term we use to describe the event of Jesusâ return into heaven after His resurrection. Three passages in the New Testament record the ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ. We will look at all three. The first passage isâ¦ NAS Mark 16:19-20 So then, when the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, He was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them, and confirmed the word by the signs that followed. 20 And they promptly reported all these instructions to Peter and his companions. And after that, Jesus Himself sent out through them from east to west the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation . {You notice that the New American Standard translation has placed v. 20 in italics; this is to indicate (along with other notes not shown here) vv. 9-20, referred to as the âlong ending of Markâ are most probably not to be considered as part of Markâs original writing. Although this professor agrees with this view, because the passage includes the word âascension,â it has been included in this particular study.} The second passage that records the ascension isâ¦ NAS Luke 24:50-51 And He led them out as far as Bethany, and He lifted up His hands and blessed them. 51 And it came about that while He was blessing them, He parted from them. The third ascension passage, doubtless the most familiar to most Christians and the focus for the majority of this study, is Acts 1:9 NAS Acts 1:9 And after He had said these things, He was lifted up while they were looking on, and a cloud received Him out of their sight. A good Bible student will ask, âwhat things?â What were the things Jesus said? The immediate context of the ascension in Acts begins in v. 6â¦ NAS Acts 1:6-8 And so when they had come together, they were asking Him, saying, âLord, is it at this time You are restoring the kingdom to Israel?â He said to them, âIt is not for you to know times or epochs which the Father has fixed by His own authority; but you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be My witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the remotest part of the earth.â 51 And it came about that while He was blessing them, He parted from them. Verses 6-8, as I believe it is easy to see, deserve an entire blog unto themselves. It could easily be said that each verse is a sermon unto itself. But for now, I would like us to look carefully at v. 8, as these are the last recorded words of Jesus before He returned to heavenâ¦ NAS Acts 1:8 but you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be My witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the remotest part of the earth.â As will be obvious to many, v. 8 is a principle application of this entire blog, if not the principle application. These words are the last thing Jesus said to His disciples and by direct extension to us. He said they would have power, and that supernatural information referred to Pentecost when the Holy Spirit came and the church began. Today every believer has been given this power. This power is the Holy Spirit which indwells every truly born again believer. And then, to His promise of power, Jesus gives every believer a mandate to be His witness. A witness where? Everywhere. âJerusalem, Samaria, and the remotest part of the worldâ correspond to our immediate location, our region, and our world. In effect, every believer is to be a witness of Christ everywhereâ¦ NAS Acts 1:9 And after He had said these things, He was lifted up while they were looking on, and a cloud received Him out of their sight. The word âascensionâ is not found in Scripture. The main verb of v. 9 (there are actually two, though the second should be seen as descriptive and therefore subordinate of the first) is the Greek word á¼ÏÎ±á½·ÏÏ ( ep-eye-ro ). á¼ÏÎ±á½·ÏÏ is a rather common word that is found 19 times in the N.T. â only by Luke and John â in a wide variety of ways, mostly positively but also negatively, in the sense of exalting oneself arrogantly (as 2 Corinthians 11:20 below). It basically means just what it says in our English Bibles: âlifted up.â The same Greek word is used in 2 Corinthians 11:20 and 1 Timothy 2:8: NAS 2 Corinthians 11:20 For you bear with anyone if he enslaves you, if he devours you, if he takes advantage of you, if he exalts himself, if he hits you in the face. NAS 1 Timothy 2:8 Therefore I want the men in every place to pray, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and dissension. In John 12:32, the Greek word for âlifted upâ is different, but the meaning is essentially the same: á½Ïá½½ÏÏ ; literally lift up, raise high (JN 3.14a); euphemistically, of the method of Christâs death by crucifixion lift up (JN 3.14b); figuratively, of honor and position uplift, exalt (LU 1.52); in a negative sense á½ÏÎ¿á¿¦Î½ á¼Î±ÏÏá½¹Î½ exalt oneself, think oneself better than others (MT 23.12). NAS John 12:32 âAnd I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to Myself.â So, nothing really esoteric with this key term. The Bible often uses relatively common terms to communicate important or even miraculous actions. The text says, âHe was lifted up.â The verb is in the passive, meaning He was lifted up by someone or something else; He didnât lift Himself up. He could have, of course, but He did not. In this case it what is called in Greek grammar a âdivine passive.â This is a beautiful way of indicating that the agent of the action of the verb is God. God lifted Jesus up in His ascensionâ¦ I am taking extra time with the term âlifted upâ to emphasize its importance. It is often easy to underestimate the power seemingly insignificant words can have in both their historical and theological contexts. âHe was lifted up.â Consider what is being said! Jesus was miraculously lifted up by the power of God and received back into heaven from which He came some thirty- three years before. Jesus Christ, God the Son, God made manifest, made visible, temporarily taking on human flesh to die for the sins of the world, now in His glorious resurrection body, left this world for the realm of heaven where He is metaphorically seated on the throne at the right hand of God the Father. He was born miraculously; He died naturally, like any other human would have died on the Cross; He resurrected miraculously; and He ascended back into heaven miraculouslyâ¦ Jesus Christ: 100% God; 100% manâ¦ The One like no otherâ¦ NAS Acts 1:9 And after He had said these things, He was lifted up while they were looking on , and a cloud received Him out of their sight. Note the clause, âwhile they were looking on.â The disciples witnessed the Ascension. Jesus ascension to heaven was a historical event. It really happened, and we know where and when it happenedâ¦ The ascension occurred at or near Bethany, a village of ancient Palestine at the foot of the Mount of Olives less than two miles east from Jerusalem. According to the New Testament, it was the site of the resurrection of Lazarus (John 11:1). As noted earlier, Luke, in his gospel (Luke wrote both the gospel of Luke and the book of Acts), reportedâ¦ NAS Luke 24:50 And He led them out as far as Bethany, and He lifted up His hands and blessed them. title: We Put the Fun in Fundamentalism
excerpt: We Put the Fun in Fundamentalism Across the country, many people tend to view Christianity as legalistic, hypocritical and boring. At Barabbas Road Church in San Diego the hope is that people would see thatâ¦
content: We Put the Fun in Fundamentalism Across the country, many people tend to view Christianity as legalistic, hypocritical and boring. At Barabbas Road Church in San Diego the hope is that people would see that fundamentalism is fun and exciting. This does not mean that Barabbas Road Church is not serious about the Bible and faith. The time and effort put into preaching and teaching the Bible at Barabbas Road Church shows that Barabbas is very serious about the ministry of the church. The hope is that the people of San Diego would see that Barabbas Road Church is a church that genuinely loves people and truly loves the Lord and his Word. What makes Barabbas Road Church in San Diego fun and exciting? Itâs probably the people of Barabbas Road church. For example, the pastoral staff is very people driven. The pastors and leaders all genuinely love people and this is contagious for the rest of the church. The people at Barabbas Road Church love each other and would lay down their lives for their brothers and sisters in Christ. The many resources that Barabbas Road Church offers, adds to the fun and exciting atmosphere as well. Ministries like Barabbas University and Small Groups all help to feed the people of Barabbas Road Church with Biblical truths and love. The time of preaching from the Bible is very serious and intense, but it is always followed with great fellowship after the service. The pastors love the people of Barabbas Road Church and love to see them fellowship with each other. The pastors also love to pour into the people of Barabbas and equipped them to grow as disciples of Christ. The fruit this is a group of people that truly loves each other and are hungry for the Word of God. Barabbas Road Church is not the typical church, yet the church is still normal in the sense. On the outside, Barabbas may look like the classic American church; however, one peek inside of a Barabbas Road Church service one will see that there is a difference. Barabbas is full of people who genuinely love people, which contributes to a friendly church environment. Most importantly, the people of Barabbas genuinely love the Lord and love to hear from the Word of God. If anyone steps into a Barabbas Road Church service on any Sunday morning â legalistic, hypocritical and boring will not be one of the words they will leave with.

content: Barabbas Road Church in San Diego â Our Mission The mission of Barabbas Road Church in San Diego is âto make âdisciple makingâ disciples through the personal investment of our lives.â The hope of Barabbas Road Church is for every person who sits in the pews of the church to know and understand the Bible. Disciples are made through the preaching and teaching of the Bible. The Ministries of Barabbas Road Church are all different; however, they all have the same goal which is to make disciples for the glory of God. Sundayâs worship service, Barabbas University and the Small Group ministry are all designed to equip the people of Barabbas Road Church to become disciples and grow as disciples of Christ. The mission is to not only make disciples but to make âdisciple makingâ disciples. This means that the goal for the people of Barabbas Road Church is for them to take what they have been taught and to teach it to other people. Therefore, each person of Barabbas Road Church is equipped and taught the Word of God, so they are then able to invest their lives into other people, teaching them and showing them the truths of the Bible. The discipleship process is as simple as asking these two questions every day: âWho is pouring into you and who are you pouring into?â By doing this, disciples will continue to be made at Barabbas Road Church and throughout San Diego. This mission is not just for the people of Barabbas Road Church in San Diego, it is for all people of San Diego. Barabbas Road Churchâs hope is for everyone in San Diego to know the God of the Bible. Different religions and different philosophies have their own ideas of who God is. Some of these groups feel as if they have figured God out. Barabbas Road Church hopes to show the people of San Diego who the true God of scripture is. Therefore, the goal is to offer the people of San Diego opportunities to hear the Word of God preached and taught. The goal is not that the people will accept what Barabbas Road is teaching, for that is up to God. The goal is to present people with the truth of the Bible. If people are going to reject this truth then the goal is for Barabbas Road Church to teach and preach the Word of God correctly, so that the people of San Diego at least know who they are rejecting.

title: Resurrection
excerpt: Resurrection NAS Matthew 28:1-6 Now after the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to look at the grave. 2 And behold, a severe earthquake had occurred,â¦
content: Resurrection NAS Matthew 28:1-6 Now after the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to look at the grave. 2 And behold, a severe earthquake had occurred, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled away the stone and sat upon it. 3 And his appearance was like lightning, and his garment as white as snow 4 and the guards shook for fear of him, and became like dead men. 5 And the angel answered and said to the women, âDo not be afraid; for I know that you are looking for Jesus who has been crucified. 6 âHe is not here, for He has risen, just as He said. Come, see the place where He was lying. Whenever I have the privilege of preaching or teaching on this passage I like to point out that all of our English translations with the exception of the NET Bible miss the passive voice in v. 6. The Greek text does not say âHe has risen,â but âHe was raised.â Grammarians have termed this a âdivine passive,â meaning that God the Father raised God the Son. But, some will surely ask, what about this verse? NAS John 10:18 âNo one has taken it away from Me, but I lay it down on My own initiative. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This commandment I received from My Father.â Someone else may ask, what about the Holy Spirit? Did He also have a part in the resurrection? The answer is yes. Admittedly, the following verse is more indirect than direct proof of the Holy Spiritâs immediate participation in the resurrection of Jesus, but it is solid. For one thing, in Romans 8:11 where the âSpiritâ and âresurrectionâ are mentioned together, the Spirit is the star of the context. Romans 8:1-17 could be titled âLife in the Spirit.â In this introductory and middle section of chapter 8, the Holy Spiritâs work in delivering the believer from the power of sin is emphasized. The reference is to the Father but the focus is on the instrumentality of the Spirit. When the subject of the resurrection is in view the focus is not so much on the historical event, but on the Spiritâs life- giving role in the resurrection. Every believer has experienced this same supernatural power in salvation, as v. 11 shows: NAS Romans 8:11 But if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit who indwells you. Thus, it is accurate to say that all three Persons of the Trinity participated in the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. That said, it must be added for the sake of more comprehensive accuracy that when the subject is studied carefully in the New Testament, it is by far most prominently the Father who raised Jesus from the dead, as the passive verb indicates in Matthew 28:6. ESV Acts 2:32 This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. NKJ Ephesians 1:20 which He worked in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly places , NAS 1 Thessalonians 1:10 and to wait for His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead, that is Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come. He is risen! And He lives! Christ Jesus lives today! âI serve a risen Savior, Heâs in the world today; I know that He is living, whatever men may say; I see His hand of mercy, I hear His voice of cheer, And just the time I need Him Heâs always near. He lives, He lives, Christ Jesus lives today! He walks with me and talks with me along lifeâs narrow way. He lives, He lives, salvation to impart! You ask me how I know He lives: He lives within my heart.â The resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ is the greatest event in the history of the world. Resurrection Sunday is the most important day of the year for the true believer in Jesus â not Christmas, as wonderful as it is, but Easter. The holiday we celebrate as Easter includes the day we call âGood Friday,â the day Jesus went to the cross. The crucifixion and the resurrection: these two great days are as two sides of the same coin; you canât really have one (the resurrection) without the other (the crucifixion). The âwages of sinâ (Romans 6:23) required a death. The crucifixion/resurrection of Christ is the cornerstone of our faith! The following verses show this: NAS 1 Corinthians 15:1, 3-4 Now I make known to you, brethren, the gospel which I preached to you, which also you received, in which also you stand, 3 For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, 4 and that He was buried, and that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, All we believe about God hinges on the resurrection of Jesus Christ: NAS 1 Corinthians 15:14 and if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is vain, your faith also is vain. NAS 1 Corinthians 15:17 and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is worthless; you are still in your sins. But, thanks be to God, He is risen! NAS Mark 16:6 And he (the angel) said to them (Mary Magdelene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome), âDo not be amazed; you are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen; He is not hereâ¦ What exactly does âresurrection mean? The English word âresurrectionâ comes from the Greek word, á¼Î½á½±ÏÏÎ±ÏÎ¹Ï ( ah-nah-stah-sis ). á¼Î½á½±ÏÏÎ±ÏÎ¹Ï is a compound noun, meaning a preposition has been prefixed to a noun; á¼Î½á½± ( ah-nah ), the prepositional prefix means again; ÏÏÎ±ÏÎ¹Ï ( stah-sis ) the following and connected noun, means stand. Thus âresurrectionâ literally means to stand again . A dead person does not stand. When Jesus died, His body was laid down horizontally. When He rose again, He stood again, vertically â bodily not spirituallyâ¦ Christianity is a physical religion. That is to say that Christianity, distinct from all other religions, places high value on the physical body in both life and death (compare Hinduism which burns the body at death. Accordingly, the physical Resurrection of Christ is the very capstone of our faith. Without it, Christianity crumbles. Jesus Christ rose physically/bodily from the grave, and because of His victory over death, we too, if we are Christians, will one day be physically/bodily raised. In 2001 there was a less-than-captivating movie that came out with the captivating title âThe Body.â The premise of this slickly anti-Christian movie was that the decomposed body of Jesus Christ had been found in a grave buried beneath a house in Jerusalem. The writers and producers of this movie â that incidentally bombed at the box-office â knew what the apostle Paul knew when he wrote, âif Christ is not risen, then our preaching is empty and your faith is also empty.â If there is a body in a grave somewhere that can be proven beyond a doubt is Jesusâ, Christianity crumbles immediately and Jesus is no different than Buddha or Krishna or Mohammed. In the 58 verses of 1 Corinthians 15, Paul gives the most extensive theological treatment of the resurrection in all of Scripture. In verses 35-49 of 1 Corinthians 15, the word âbodyâ and the neuter pronouns referring to it are found no less than 18 times. The Greek word for âbody,â Ïá¿¶Î¼Î± ( so-mah ), is used 146 times in the NT, almost every time in reference to a physical , material body. The evidence is overwhelming; you have to stubbornly will to ignore it in order to argue the fact that Scripture declares the physical, bodily resurrection of the Lord Jesus. title: Barabbas Road Church in San Diego Christianity Classes

content: Barabbas Road Church in San Diego Offers Many Classes on Christianity One of the most popular resources that Barabbas Road Church in San Diego offers is Barabbas University. Barabbas University is a self-proclaimed and unaccredited University that is run by Barabbas Road Church. Barabbas University is for Christians living in the San Diego area who want a deeper understanding the Bible and Christianity. Barabbas University is also for people who may not be Christian but are interested in learning more about Christianity. Barabbas University is a great way for a person to get a Christian education and learn more about the Bible and who God really is. The classes at Barabbas University help a person dig into the truths of the Bible and take oneâs faith to a deeper level that they might not otherwise understand. Barabbas University classes are held on Sunday and Tuesday evenings. The two classes that are held on Sunday nights are a foundation class and a Christian counseling class. The foundation class walks through systematic theology. Also, the class spends some time going all the major world views. This class is a fun and interactive class that teaches the basic truths of the Bible that are valuable for all Christians. The Christian counseling class begins after the Foundation class; therefore, a person can go to each class on a Sunday night. The Christian counseling class walks the class through the curriculum from IBCD which stands for the Institute for Biblical Counseling and discipleship. There are 40 classes in this program and once completed a student will receive a credited Christian Counseling certificate. This class is for those who want to learn how to use the Bible to counsel people knowing scripture is sufficient to counsel. This class will help equip students to counsel other people in the church and other areas. On Tuesday nightâs the other two classes offered are Theology 201 and Apologetics 201. The Theology 201 class is a step up from the Foundations class. In this class Pastor Matt digs deeper into the foundations of Christianity as he goes through books like, âCalvinâs Institutesâ by John Calvin and âStrange Fire,â by John MacArthur. Apologetics 201 is the most popular class as Pastor Matt equips the class to be able to handle the intellectual skepticism and Gnosticism found throughout the world, especially in the culture of San Diego. Pastor Matt teaches through the Bible and various books to teach on presuppositional apologetics. In this class Pastor Matt looks to answer questions like, âCan truth be knownâ and âHow can we know that truth exists?â The mission of Barabbas Road Church in San Diego to make disciples is simply not a slogan to put up on a banner. Barabbas Road Church is truly passionate about making disciples for Godâs glory and the evidence of this can be found in commitment to Barabbas University.

title: Jesus and the Cross

content: Jesus and the Cross WHY THE CROSS? The subtitle of this blog is âJesus and the Cross and Godâs Righteousness. NAS Romans 3:21-26 But now apart from the Law the righteousness of God has been manifested, being witnessed by the Law and the Prophets, 22 even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all those who believe; for there is no distinction; 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 being justified as a gift by His grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus; 25 whom God displayed publicly as a propitiation in His blood through faith. This was to demonstrate His righteousness, because in the forbearance of God He passed over the sins previously committed; 26 for the demonstration, I say , of His righteousness at the present time, that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. The crucifixion of Jesus Christ was the climax of redemptive history, the focal point of Godâs plan of salvation. The whole of Godâs redeeming work culminated in the Cross, where the Lord Jesus bore the sins of the worldâ¦ NAS Matthew 27:21-22 But the governor answered and said to them, âWhich of the two do you want me to release for you?â And they said, âBarabbas.â 22 Pilate said to them, âThen what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?â They all said, âLet Him be crucified!â And they crucified Him. And they crudely nailed His precious hands and feet on a wooden crossâ¦âand they crucified Himââ¦ Question: âWhy the cross? Why did Jesus have to go to the Cross? Just like the question, âWhy did Jesus come in the first place?â there are a number of legitimate answers one could give. One is, âThe Cross was the ultimate expression of Godâs love for mankind.â Surely that is one of the main reasons why Jesus had to go to the Cross. But I am going to suggest to you that the primary reason Jesus had to go to the Cross was to demonstrate Godâs righteousness. As I believe you will see, I have scriptural support for that claim. Romans 3:21-26 is a magnificent passage of Scripture that deals with the crucifixion of Christ from a theological perspective â theological as opposed to a historical perspective. The historical perspective is found, for example, in Matthew 27:24-35aâ¦ NAS Matthew 27:24-35 And when Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but rather that a riot was starting, he took water and washed his hands in front of the multitude, saying, âI am innocent of this Manâs blood; see to that yourselves.â 25 And all the people answered and said, âHis blood be on us and on our children!â 26 Then he released Barabbas for them; but after having Jesus scourged, he delivered Him to be crucified. 27 Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the Praetorium and gathered the whole Roman cohort around Him. 28 And they stripped Him, and put a scarlet robe on Him. 29 And after weaving a crown of thorns, they put it on His head, and a reed in His right hand; and they kneeled down before Him and mocked Him, saying, âHail, King of the Jews!â 30 And they spat on Him, and took the reed and began to beat Him on the head. 31 And after they had mocked Him, they took His robe off and put His garments on Him, and led Him away to crucify Him . 32 And as they were coming out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon, whom they pressed into service to bear His cross. 33 And when they had come to a place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull, 34 they gave Him wine to drink mingled with gall; and after tasting it , He was unwilling to drink. 35 And when they had crucified Him, they divided up His garments among themselves, casting lots; While the two terms â theological and historical â are distinctive, they are complimentary. A historical perspective would be one that looks at the Cross primarily in terms of its historical relevance. It would be a practical study, concerned mainly with how the event happened. A theological perspective, on the other hand, while not divorced of historical significance, is concerned with the events of the crucifixion in abstract terms. It would focus on why it happened. A theological perspective deals with the spiritual meaning of the Cross. We might say a historical study would look at the Cross from manâs point of view, while a theological study would look at the Cross from Godâs point of view. Our study this week will look at the Cross through Godâs eyes, and by so doing we will see its spiritual relationship to us. Understanding the Cross from a theological perspective is fundamental to us accurately comprehending our salvation. âJesus and the Cross and Godâs Righteousnessâ: A look at the Cross from Godâs point of viewâ¦ Romans 2:21-25 gives us the meaning of Easter. When man sinned he incurred Godâs wrath. A holy, sinless God cannot tolerate sin. Therefore, there was a spiritual separation between God and man. Manâs religions throughout history have tried in vain to bridge that gap, but the only way is Jesus. Because God loves man He sent His Son to bridge the gap. The only way Godâs wrath over sin could be appeased was for there to be an atoning sacrificial death, a death so powerful that it would cover and take away manâs sin. Only Christâs blood, the blood of God, could do this. Through the Cross, Godâs holiness and righteousness were preserved and a way was made for man to be accepted. Through Christ alone man is declared righteousâ¦ In order to understand Jesus and the cross, we must understand Godâs righteousness. One of the major themes of Romans, if not the major theme â is righteousness. The word in different forms is repeated more than 60 times in Romans. Righteousness in human terms, it may be accurately said, is conformity to the claims of a higher authority. âRighteousness stands in opposition to lawlessness. In both the O.T. and N.T., righteousness is the state of man that is commanded by God. It is what is required to stand the test of His judgment (2 Cor 3:9; 6:14; Eph 4:24). Righteousness is conformity to all that He commands or appointsâ (Zodhiates/TAR). Said succinctly, righteousness is right standing with God, something man on his own without the help of a gracious Savior could never hope to achieve. Look at Romans 3:25-26 again (emphasis added)â¦ NKJ Romans 3:25-26 ( Jesus ) whom God set forth as a propitiation by His blood, through faith, to demonstrate His righteousness , because in His forbearance God had passed over the sins that were previously committed, 26 to demonstrate at the present time His righteousness , that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Here we have no less than the purpose of the cross: to demonstrate God the Fatherâs righteousness. To whom? To everyone, to His entire creation. The word âdemonstrateâ is very interesting. The Greek word á¼Î½Î´Îµá½·ÎºÎ½ÏÎ¼Î¹ ( en-deik-nu-mi ) means to direct attention to or cause something to become known; to show, to demonstrate, to display conduct that affects another, to prove. I encourage you to contemplate Easter in light of this word. I believe such solemn meditation will enhance our already deep appreciation of our dear Lord. In order to possess the righteousness of God, we must have faith in Jesus and Jesus alone and be saved by the blood of Christ. It is not ours, but Christâs righteousness we possess. Righteousness is available to all. By dying on the cross, Christ paid for the sins of the whole world, and His righteousness is available to the whole world. This does not mean, of course, that everyone will be saved. Righteousness is realized only by those who place their trust in Christ alone. title: Church in San Diego Partners with CAPS
excerpt: Church in San Diego Partners with CAPS One ministry that Barabbas Road Church in San Diego is involved with outside of the church is an organization called CAPS. CAPS stands for College Area Pregnancy Services. CAPS isâ¦
content: Church in San Diego Partners with CAPS One ministry that Barabbas Road Church in San Diego is involved with outside of the church is an organization called CAPS. CAPS stands for College Area Pregnancy Services. CAPS is a medical clinic that provides early medical help and peer counseling to those facing unexpected pregnancies. The counseling that CAPS offers includes: Options counseling (Abortion Procedures and Risks, Adoption Education and Parenting Education and Support); Pregnancy counseling (Education on Fetal Development and Physician Referrals); Relationship Counseling (Sexuality Issues, Relationship Issues and STD Risk Education). CAPS has multiple offices located around the San Diego area, including an office close to the church in Pacific Beach. Barabbas Road Church promotes and gives to this organization because it is a tremendous blessing to the area. One of the main benefits of this clinic is that every woman that comes through the clinic is given the Gospel. The women are also taught the value of human life based upon the image of God. The clinic is there to counsel women, to support them and to provide them with accurate information about pregnancy, fetal development, lifestyle issues, and related concerns. Over the past year, 99% of the women that came into the clinic and saw an ultrasound stopped the abortion process. This is why Barabbas Road church is so supportive of this organization. This clinic is for anyone, regardless of age, race, income, nationality, religious affiliation, disability or other arbitrary circumstances. Everyone is welcomed to come into the clinic to get help. Even if a person just wants an Ultrasound, the clinic offers this service as well. What makes the clinic even more special is that all of its services are free. This is also why it is important for individuals and churches like Barabbas Road church to support organizations like CAPS. The Caps offices are surrounded by advertising and support for Planned Parenthood; therefore, Barabbas Church Road in San Diego believes the free services of CAPS are very important to the community. This is why Barabbas Road church does not hesitate to promote CAPS and to include CAPS in Barabbas Road Church activities. The mission of Barabbas Road Church is âto make âdisciple makingâ disciples through the personal investment of our lives.â Investing time and money into an organization like CAPS is part of worship in the disciple making process. Therefore, Barabbas Road church is passionate about the work that CAPS is doing.

title: Lamb Selection Day

content: Lamb Selection Day In this writing I will suggest that instead of âPalm Sunday,â the time-honored term for the Sunday before Resurrection Sunday, a better, more biblical title might be âLamb Selection Day.â NAS John 12:12-19 On the next day the great multitude who had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took the branches of the palm trees, and went out to meet Him, and began to cry out, âHosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel.â And Jesus, finding a young donkey, sat on it; as it is written, âFear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your King is coming, seated on a donkeyâs colt.â These things His disciples did not understand at the first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written of Him, and that they had done these things to Him. And so the multitude who were with Him when He called Lazarus out of the tomb, and raised him from the dead, were bearing Him witness. For this cause also the multitude went and met Him, because they heard that He had performed this sign. The Pharisees therefore said to one another, âYou see that you are not doing any good; look, the world has gone after Him.â Nelsonâs New Christian Dictionary , an ecumenical source, includes this entry on âPalm Sunday: âPalm Sunday,â also called âPassion Sunday,â is the Sunday beginning Holy Week (âPalm Sundayâ to Easter), commemorating Jesusâ triumphal entry into Jerusalem and marking the beginning of Holy Week. The distinctive ceremony of Palm Sunday services is the blessing of palms and a procession reenacting the biblical events on this day.â Obviously this ecumenical dictionary is taking a Catholic slant. Most Baptists do not officially make this big of a deal about Palm Sunday. That is, by having a âblessing of the palmsâ and a âprocession reenacting the biblical events on this dayâ in a manner comparable to Catholics, Lutherans, some Methodists, and some Presbyterians. It is not my purpose in this blog to discuss the merits of Palm Sunday. I personally do not have a problem with Palm Sunday celebrations. Itâs in the Bible, as the passage from John above shows. There was a day in which Jesus entered Jerusalem and people celebrated using Palm branches. Surely I am not going to win this argument, but I want to suggest in this installment is that there may be a more biblically accurate name for this day: âLamb Selection Day.â Over my years of Bible study, I have come to see the inherent significance of the Jewish feasts to âEaster.â I put quotation marks around the word because the more I study and think about the subject, the less I embrace the word. The word âEasterâ is a topic for another blog, but for now let me just say that its highly questionable etymology notwithstanding, we probably wouldnât be using the word today if it were not for the King James Bibleâs mistranslation of Acts 12:4, where âEasterâ should have been translated âPassover.â the Greek word is Ïá½±ÏÏÎ± ( pah-skah ); it means Passover. As so many New Testament doctrines, âPalm Sundayâ has its roots in the Old Testament. NAS Exodus 12:1-6 Now the LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, 2 âThis month shall be the beginning of months for you; it is to be the first month of the year to you. 3 âSpeak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, âOn the tenth of this month they are each one to take a lamb for themselves, according to their fathersâ households, a lamb for each household. 4 âNow if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his neighbor nearest to his house are to take one according to the number of persons in them ; according to what each man should eat, you are to divide the lamb. 5 âYour lamb shall be an unblemished male a year old; you may take it from the sheep or from the goats. 6 âAnd you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month, then the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel is to kill it at twilight. This, of course, is the biblical preparation for the great Jewish feast of Passover. The Passover event is the historical reference to Godâs deliverance of Israel from the bondage of Egypt. âPassoverâ is the English word for the Hebrew word, ×¤Ö¼Ö¶×¡Ö·× ( pey-sahk ) which literally means âto spring,â âjump,â or âpass over.â NAS Exodus 12:13 âAnd the blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you live; and when I see the blood I will pass over (×¤Ö¼Ö¶×¡Ö·×) you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt. The first part of Exodus 12 chronicles âLamb Selection Day.â To the Jew, âtwilightâ most probably meant precisely 3 PM. At 3 PM (most probably), the shofar (ramâs horn) was sounded and the main daily sacrifice was offered. This assured religious Jews, wherever they may be, that God, according to His promise to Abraham, would provide a sacrifice for sin (because man couldnât)â¦ NAS Genesis 15:7-10, 17 And He said to him, âI am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to possess it.â 8 And he said, âO Lord God, how may I know that I shall possess it?â 9 So He said to him, âBring Me a three year old heifer, and a three year old female goat, and a three year old ram, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon.â 10 Then he brought all these to Him and cut them in two, and laid each half opposite the other; but he did not cut the birds. 17 And it came about when the sun had set, that it was very dark, and behold, there appeared a smoking oven and a flaming torch which passed between these pieces. This is what some Bible teachers term the âblood trail.â Normally, in the cutting (the appropriate term commonly used) of an ancient covenant, both parties walked barefooted through the blood together. This was to signify that should one break the covenant, the other could lawfully do him what they had done to the animals and birds. By walking the âblood trailâ alone, God, in effect, was saying, âIâll pay the price when you break the covenant, an awesome picture of the divinely initiated relationship of God and the believer. Notice the text in Exodus 12:4 says a lamb âwithout blemish.â The lamb selected was to be as close to perfect as possible. This pointed to the incomparable day when a perfect sacrifice would be offered for the sins of the world: NAS John 1:29 The next day he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, âBehold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world! NAS Hebrews 4:15 For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but One who has been tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin. Jesus was the sinless sacrifice, the Lamb of God without blemish who took away the sin of the world, so that anyone who believes receives salvation. title: What Age People Make up Barabbas Road Church in San Diego?
excerpt: What Age People Make up Barabbas Road Church in San Diego? The people of Barabbas Road Church in San Diego are passionate about making disciples for the glory of God. The church will continue to have plenty ofâ¦
content: What Age People Make up Barabbas Road Church in San Diego? The people of Barabbas Road Church in San Diego are passionate about making disciples for the glory of God. The church will continue to have plenty of opportunities to make disciples in the future because of the number of families that attend the church. One reason there are so many families is because many families are starting and growing at Barabbas Road Church. Because of the location of the church, there are a number of singles that attend the church. What has happened is that the singles are marrying each other and starting their own families. Over the past three years, 40 marriage ceremonies have been done at the church, and now those married couples are starting to have kids. Another advantage of the churchâs location is that it attracts a lot of young professionals. The majority of the people who attend Barabbas Road Church are singles and married couples between the ages of 25 to 35. Even though the main demographic of the church is a young group, the church does have many people of various ages who attend and enjoy worshipping at Barabbas Road Church. Although Barabbas road church is made up of different types of people, they all have one main thing in common: the desire to hear the Word of God preached every Sunday morning. This is how God is growing the church as people are growing as disciples of Christ and in return many more disciples are being made. Barabbas Road Church offers many ministries that different age groups can benefit from. For example, the Menâs ministry meets every month and discusses the role of men in the church. This group is for both single and married men and discusses what God has created men for. Likewise, the women meet each month and discuss the role of women in the church. This group learns about what God has created women for and it is for single and married women. The mission of Barabbas Road Church is âto make âdisciple makingâ disciples through the personal investment of our lives.â Ministries like the Childrenâs ministry, Singles ministry, Menâs ministry, Womenâs ministry, Momâs ministry, Marriage ministry and Barabbas University all are for the purpose to make and grow disciples of all ages for the Glory of God. Although, the ages that make up Barabbas Road church lean towards the younger generations, the focus and desire of Barabbas Road Church is to make disciples of all age groups.

title: BE Ye Holy
excerpt: BE Ye Holy I could easily write ten single-spaced pages on âholyâ or âholiness.â So, please consider this entry only an introduction to the subject. The title for this weekâs writing, however, âBe ye holy,â many willâ¦
content: BE Ye Holy I could easily write ten single-spaced pages on âholyâ or âholiness.â So, please consider this entry only an introduction to the subject. The title for this weekâs writing, however, âBe ye holy,â many will recognize comes from 1 Peter 1:15 and 16. I use the old King James Bible here no only because it was from this version that I first memorized these words, but also because I believe that in some places in Scripture the 17th century vocabulary may be seen as more poetic and therefore forceful. âBe ye holyâ may be such a euphonic example: KJV 1 Peter 1:15-16 But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation; 16 Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy. Peter is referencing an Old Testament verse from Leviticus 19: ESV Leviticus 19:2 âSpeak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy. I hope to show in this abbreviated study the importance of Peterâs words for us today. In our post-modern and at the same time pagan culture, in which the profane and immoral are commonplace, God wants us to be holy. âIn all manner of conversationâ means our conduct, our behavior, really everything we say and do. âHolyâ in our English Bibles is found no less than 649 times from 581 verses (according to BibleWorks [not a typo] electronic Bible program; other sources may vary slightly). The reason I specify âEnglishâ is because the Hebrew and Greek words are often used more times but are not always translated by the word âholy.â They could, for example, be translated âsanctificationâ or âsaint.â Whether found in the Old Testament or the New Testament, these three words come from the same root. The translations of that root depend on the context in which it is used. âHolyâ is an adjective. Adjectives describe. The main Hebrew adjective is ×§×Ö¹×××© ( kah-dosh ). HALOT, the leading Hebrew lexicon, defines it, â holy, commanding respect, awesome , treated with respect, removed from profane usage; holy, singled out, consecrated for â (the italicized words should be seen as more central â TAR). That little last word, âfor,â is noteworthy. People and things are not just holy or sanctified; they are sanctified for something. You have to be careful making too much of root meanings of words. Sometimes they are accurate indicators of meaning; other times not. Context, more than lexical definitions or root information, determines ultimate meaning. In the case of âholy,â in my humble opinion, consulting the root meaning is helpful. The root meaning of ×§×Ö¹×××© includes these descriptive ideas: a sacred place or thing, sanctify wholly . Note again the last word. In the Bible, a person or thing is either holy or not; there is no middle ground, no partial holiness. Sadly, this does not square with our human tendency to rationalize our own behavior. The main Greek adjective âholyâ is á¼Î³Î¹Î¿Ï ( ha-gee-os ). BDAG, the foremost Greek lexicon, defines á¼Î³Î¹Î¿Ï as â pert. to being dedicated or consecrated to the service of God.â In Bauer, Danker, Ardnt, and Gingrichâs discussion of á¼Î³Î¹Î¿Ï , they explain that the word shades over into these adjectives, pure, perfect , and worthy of God . ESV Romans 12:1 I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. ESV 2 Peter 3:11 Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, It is my intention that by going over the basic meanings of both the Hebrew and Greek words, you will get a greater understanding and appreciation of what exactly the Bible means when it says believers are to âbe holy.â Itâs hard to be something when we donât know what it is. What does it look like to be holy? Hopefully this study will help us to see. The first time the English word âholyâ appears in the Bible is in Exodus 3:5: NAS Exodus 3:5 Then He said, âDo not come near here; remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.â Back to 1 Peter. Notice that v. 15 states that God Himself is holy, and in v. 16 it says that the reason we are to be holy is because God is holy. Letâs consider the fact of Godâs holiness and then look more closely at what the word âholyâ means in related doctrines of the Bible. Yahweh (popularly accepted as the O.T. name for God) is emphatically holy: NAS 1 Samuel 2:2 âThere is no one holy like the LORD, Indeed, there is no one besides Thee, Nor is there any rock like our God. Most scholars would agree that a triple repetition of a word or thought is the ultimate emphasis in Scripture. NAS Isaiah 6:3 And one called out to another and said, âHoly, Holy, Holy, is the LORD of hosts, The whole earth is full of His glory.â There is no question the Bible declares over and over that God is holy: NAS Isaiah 43:14 Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, âFor your sake I have sent to Babylon, And will bring them all down as fugitives, Even the Chaldeans, into the ships in which they rejoice. NAS Isaiah 45:11 Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and his Maker: âAsk Me about the things to come concerning My sons, And you shall commit to Me the work of My hands. Godâs name is holy: NAS Leviticus 20:3 âI will also set My face against that man and will cut him off from among his people, because he has given some of his offspring to Molech, so as to defile My sanctuary and to profane My holy name. NAS 1 Chronicles 16:10 Glory in His holy name; Let the heart of those who seek the LORD be glad. NAS Matthew 6:9 âPray, then, in this way: âOur Father who art in heaven, Hallowed be Thy name. âHallowedâ is from the same Greek word as âHoly.â When we hallow Godâs name we are setting it apart from all other names. Perhaps the best single definition of biblical holiness is separateness: NAS Joshua 24:19 Then Joshua said to the people, âYou will not be able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God. He is a jealous God; He will not forgive your transgression or your sins. NAS Leviticus 11:44 âFor I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy. And you shall not make yourselves unclean with any of the swarming things that swarm on the earth. âHolyâ is separate and distinguished from anything profane, anything sinful or ungodly: ESV Leviticus 10:9 âDrink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations. The nation of Israel was holy, set apart from other nations: NAS Exodus 19:6 and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.â These are the words that you shall speak to the sons of Israel.â NAS Deuteronomy 7:6 âFor you are a holy people to the LORD your God; the LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His own possession out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth. Note âchosen out.â As a commonplace analogy, when we go to the sore to buy something, we chose that something out of the other things. On a spiritual level when God saves us, He chooses us, and that choosing makes us separate, spiritually set apart from the world: NAS John 15:16 âYou did not choose Me, but I chose you, and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain, that whatever you ask of the Father in My name, He may give to you. Note here another definitive characteristic of holy, i.e., we are not simply chosen, we are chosen for a purpose: âThat you should go and bear fruit.â Similarly, O.T. priests were chosen and âset apartâ for service to the Lord: NAS 1 Chronicles 23:13 The sons of Amram were Aaron and Moses. And Aaron was set apart to sanctify him as most holy, he and his sons forever, to burn incense before the LORD, to minister to Him and to bless in His name forever.
